Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall, / And by the doom of death end woes and all.
Go on, Solinus, bring about my ruin, and end my sorrows and everything else with a sentence of death.

Merchant of Syracusa, plead no more. / I am not partial to infringe our laws. / The enmity and discord which of late / Sprung from the rancorous outrage of your Duke / To merchants, our well-dealing countrymen, / Who, wanting guilders to redeem their lives, / Have seal'd his rigorous statutes with their bloods, / Excludes all pity from our threat'ning looks. / For since the mortal and intestine jars / 'Twixt thy seditious countrymen and us, / It hath in solemn synods been decreed, / Both by the Syracusians and ourselves, / To admit no traffic to our adverse towns; / Nay more, if any born at Ephesus / Be seen at Syracusian marts and fairs; / Again, if any Syracusian born / Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies, / His goods confiscate to the Duke's dispose, / Unless a thousand marks be levied / To quit the penalty and to ransom him. / Thy substance, valued at the highest rate, / Cannot amount unto a hundred marks; / Therefore by law thou art condemn'd to die.

Merchant of Syracuse, stop pleading. I am not inclined to bend our laws. Your Duke has lately treated our honest merchants with spiteful cruelty: when they could not find the money to buy back their lives, he sealed his harsh laws with their blood. That hostility and conflict rules out any pity in my face. Ever since the deadly civil quarrels between your rebellious countrymen and us, it has been decreed in formal councils, by both the Syracusans and ourselves, that there will be no trade between our hostile cities. More than that: if anyone born in Ephesus is seen at the markets and fairs of Syracuse, or if anyone born in Syracuse comes into the bay of Ephesus, he dies, and his goods are seized for the Duke to dispose of, unless a thousand marks are raised to pay the penalty and ransom him. Your property, valued at the very highest, comes to less than a hundred marks. So by law you are condemned to die.
Yet this my comfort; when your words are done, / My woes end likewise with the evening sun.
Yet I have this comfort: when your sentence is carried out, my sorrows will end with the setting sun.
Well, Syracusian, say in brief the cause / Why thou departedst from thy native home, / And for what cause thou cam'st to Ephesus.
Well, man of Syracuse, tell me briefly why you left your home, and why you came to Ephesus.

A heavier task could not have been impos'd / Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable; / Yet, that the world may witness that my end / Was wrought by nature, not by vile offence, / I'll utter what my sorrow gives me leave. / In Syracusa was I born, and wed / Unto a woman happy but for me, / And by me, had not our hap been bad. / With her I liv'd in joy; our wealth increas'd / By prosperous voyages I often made / To Epidamnum, till my factor's death, / And the great care of goods at random left, / Drew me from kind embracements of my spouse; / From whom my absence was not six months old / Before herself (almost at fainting under / The pleasing punishment that women bear) / Had made provision for her following me, / And soon and safe arrived where I was. / There had she not been long but she became / A joyful mother of two goodly sons, / And, which was strange, the one so like the other / As could not be distinguish'd but by names. / That very hour, and in the self-same inn, / A mean woman was delivered / Of such a burden, male twins, both alike. / Those, for their parents were exceeding poor, / I bought, and brought up to attend my sons. / My wife, not meanly proud of two such boys, / Made daily motions for our home return. / Unwilling I agreed; alas, too soon / We came aboard. / A league from Epidamnum had we sail'd / Before the always-wind-obeying deep / Gave any tragic instance of our harm; / But longer did we not retain much hope; / For what obscured light the heavens did grant / Did but convey unto our fearful minds / A doubtful warrant of immediate death, / Which though myself would gladly have embrac'd, / Yet the incessant weepings of my wife, / Weeping before for what she saw must come, / And piteous plainings of the pretty babes, / That mourn'd for fashion, ignorant what to fear, / Forc'd me to seek delays for them and me. / And this it was (for other means was none). / The sailors sought for safety by our boat, / And left the ship, then sinking-ripe, to us. / My wife, more careful for the latter-born, / Had fast'ned him unto a small spare mast, / Such as sea-faring men provide for storms. / To him one of the other twins was bound, / Whilst I had been like heedful of the other. / The children thus dispos'd, my wife and I, / Fixing our eyes on whom our care was fix'd, / Fast'ned ourselves at either end the mast, / And, floating straight, obedient to the stream, / Was carried towards Corinth, as we thought. / At length the sun, gazing upon the earth, / Dispers'd those vapours that offended us, / And by the benefit of his wished light / The seas wax'd calm, and we discovered / Two ships from far, making amain to us, / Of Corinth that, of Epidaurus this. / But ere they came—O, let me say no more! / Gather the sequel by that went before.

No harder task could be set me than to speak of griefs too great for words. Still, so that the world may see my death was caused by natural love and not by any wicked crime, I will tell as much as my sorrow allows. I was born in Syracuse, and married a woman who would have been happy if it weren't for me, and would have been happy with me if our luck had not been bad. I lived with her in joy, and our wealth grew through the profitable voyages I often made to Epidamnum. Then my agent there died, and the need to look after goods left unattended drew me away from my wife's loving arms. I had been gone less than six months when she, though nearly fainting under the pleasant burden that women carry, arranged to follow me, and arrived safe and soon where I was. She had not been there long before she became the joyful mother of two fine sons, and, strangely, the one so like the other that they could only be told apart by their names. In that same hour, at the very same inn, a poor woman gave birth to identical twin boys. Because their parents were extremely poor, I bought them and brought them up to serve my sons. My wife, very proud of our two boys, kept pressing for us to go home. I agreed, unwillingly, and all too soon we went aboard. We had sailed three miles from Epidamnum before the sea, which always obeys the wind, gave any sign of the disaster to come. But after that we didn't keep much hope, for the dim light the heavens gave us only told our frightened minds that death was near. I would gladly have accepted it, but my wife's constant weeping, as she cried in advance for what she saw was coming, and the pitiful wailing of the babies, who cried because she did without knowing what to fear, forced me to look for ways to delay death for them and me. This was what happened, since there was no other way out. The sailors escaped in our lifeboat and left the ship, ready to sink, to us. My wife, more anxious about the younger twin, had tied him to a small spare mast of the kind sailors carry for storms, and with him one of the other twins. I had done the same for the other two. With the children arranged like that, my wife and I, keeping our eyes on the ones we cared for, tied ourselves to either end of the mast, and, floating with the current, were carried towards Corinth, or so we thought. At last the sun shone on the earth and broke up the mists that had troubled us. In that welcome light the sea grew calm, and we saw two ships racing towards us from far off, one from Corinth, the other from Epidaurus. But before they reached us... O, let me say no more! Guess the rest from what came before.
Nay, forward, old man, do not break off so, / For we may pity, though not pardon thee.
No, go on, old man, don't stop there. I may pity you, even if I cannot pardon you.

O, had the gods done so, I had not now / Worthily term'd them merciless to us. / For, ere the ships could meet by twice five leagues, / We were encountered by a mighty rock, / Which being violently borne upon, / Our helpful ship was splitted in the midst; / So that, in this unjust divorce of us, / Fortune had left to both of us alike / What to delight in, what to sorrow for. / Her part, poor soul, seeming as burdened / With lesser weight, but not with lesser woe, / Was carried with more speed before the wind, / And in our sight they three were taken up / By fishermen of Corinth, as we thought. / At length another ship had seiz'd on us; / And, knowing whom it was their hap to save, / Gave healthful welcome to their ship-wrack'd guests, / And would have reft the fishers of their prey, / Had not their bark been very slow of sail; / And therefore homeward did they bend their course. / Thus have you heard me sever'd from my bliss, / That by misfortunes was my life prolong'd / To tell sad stories of my own mishaps.

O, if the gods had pitied us, I would not now rightly be calling them merciless! Before the ships could get within ten leagues of us, we were driven onto a great rock. We struck it so violently that our helpful mast was split in two, so that in this cruel separation Fortune left each of us something to delight in and something to grieve for. Her half, poor soul, carrying less weight though no less sorrow, was swept along faster by the wind, and before our eyes the three of them were picked up by fishermen from Corinth, as we thought. At last another ship rescued us. Knowing who they had saved, the crew made us welcome, shipwrecked as we were, and would have taken the others from the fishermen if their ship had not been so slow. So they turned and sailed for home. Now you have heard how I was parted from my happiness, and how bad luck kept me alive only to tell the sad story of my own misfortunes.
And for the sake of them thou sorrowest for, / Do me the favour to dilate at full / What have befall'n of them and thee till now.
For the sake of those you are grieving for, do me the favour of telling me in full what has happened to them and to you since then.

My youngest boy, and yet my eldest care, / At eighteen years became inquisitive / After his brother, and importun'd me / That his attendant, so his case was like, / Reft of his brother, but retain'd his name, / Might bear him company in the quest of him; / Whom whilst I laboured of a love to see, / I hazarded the loss of whom I lov'd. / Five summers have I spent in farthest Greece, / Roaming clean through the bounds of Asia, / And, coasting homeward, came to Ephesus, / Hopeless to find, yet loath to leave unsought / Or that or any place that harbours men. / But here must end the story of my life; / And happy were I in my timely death, / Could all my travels warrant me they live.

My youngest boy, though he is my eldest care, began asking about his brother when he was eighteen. He begged me to let his servant, who was in the same situation, robbed of his brother but keeping his name, go with him to search for him. Because I longed to see the son I had lost, I risked losing the one I loved. I have spent five summers in the furthest parts of Greece, travelling right through Asia Minor, and coming home along the coast I reached Ephesus. I had no hope of finding them, yet I could not bear to leave this or any other inhabited place unsearched. But here my life's story must end. I would be happy to die now, if all my travels could assure me they are alive.

Hapless Egeon, whom the fates have mark'd / To bear the extremity of dire mishap; / Now, trust me, were it not against our laws, / Against my crown, my oath, my dignity, / Which princes, would they, may not disannul, / My soul should sue as advocate for thee. / But though thou art adjudged to the death, / And passed sentence may not be recall'd / But to our honour's great disparagement, / Yet will I favour thee in what I can. / Therefore, merchant, I'll limit thee this day / To seek thy health by beneficial help. / Try all the friends thou hast in Ephesus; / Beg thou, or borrow, to make up the sum, / And live; if no, then thou art doom'd to die. / Jailer, take him to thy custody.

Unlucky Egeon, marked out by the fates to suffer the worst misfortune! Believe me, if it were not against our laws, my crown, my oath and my dignity, which princes cannot cancel even if they wish to, I would plead for you myself. But though you are sentenced to death, and the sentence cannot be withdrawn without great damage to my honour, I will still help you as far as I can. So, merchant, I give you this one day to save yourself by finding help. Try every friend you have in Ephesus. Beg or borrow to make up the sum, and live. If not, you are condemned to die. Jailer, take him into custody.
Hopeless and helpless doth Egeon wend, / But to procrastinate his lifeless end.
Without hope or help, Egeon goes off, only to put off the death that will end his life.

Therefore give out you are of Epidamnum, / Lest that your goods too soon be confiscate. / This very day a Syracusian merchant / Is apprehended for arrival here, / And, not being able to buy out his life, / According to the statute of the town / Dies ere the weary sun set in the west. / There is your money that I had to keep.

So say you come from Epidamnum, or your goods will be seized straight away. This very day a merchant from Syracuse has been arrested for landing here, and since he can't buy his life, by the law of this town he dies before the tired sun sets in the west. Here is the money I was keeping for you.

Go bear it to the Centaur, where we host, / And stay there, Dromio, till I come to thee. / Within this hour it will be dinnertime; / Till that, I'll view the manners of the town, / Peruse the traders, gaze upon the buildings, / And then return and sleep within mine inn, / For with long travel I am stiff and weary. / Get thee away.

Take it to the Centaur, where we're staying, and wait there till I come, Dromio. It will be dinnertime within the hour. Until then I'll look at the ways of the town, study the traders, gaze at the buildings, then go back and sleep at the inn, because I'm stiff and tired from travelling so long. Off you go.
Many a man would take you at your word, / And go indeed, having so good a mean.
Many a man would take you at your word and go off for good, with such a good means of doing it.

A trusty villain, sir, that very oft, / When I am dull with care and melancholy, / Lightens my humour with his merry jests. / What, will you walk with me about the town, / And then go to my inn and dine with me?
He's a trustworthy rascal, sir. Very often, when I'm low with worry and gloom, he cheers me up with his jokes. Will you walk round the town with me, then come back to my inn and have dinner with me?

I am invited, sir, to certain merchants, / Of whom I hope to make much benefit. / I crave your pardon. Soon, at five o'clock, / Please you, I'll meet with you upon the mart, / And afterward consort you till bedtime. / My present business calls me from you now.

I'm invited by some merchants, sir, and I hope to do good business with them. Please excuse me. Later, at five o'clock, if you like, I'll meet you at the market and keep you company till bedtime. My business calls me away now.
Farewell till then: I will go lose myself, / And wander up and down to view the city.
Goodbye till then. I'll go and lose myself and wander up and down looking at the city.
Sir, I commend you to your own content.
Sir, I wish you all the contentment you could want.

He that commends me to mine own content / Commends me to the thing I cannot get. / I to the world am like a drop of water / That in the ocean seeks another drop, / Who, failing there to find his fellow forth, / Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself. / So I, to find a mother and a brother, / In quest of them, unhappy, lose myself.

He wishes me contentment, the one thing I cannot get. In this world I am like a drop of water searching the ocean for another drop: failing to find its fellow, it falls in, unseen and searching, and loses itself. So I, seeking a mother and a brother, lose myself in the search, unhappy as I am.
Here comes the almanac of my true date. / What now? How chance thou art return'd so soon?
Here comes the calendar of my own life. What's this? How come you're back so soon?

Return'd so soon? rather approach'd too late. / The capon burns, the pig falls from the spit; / The clock hath strucken twelve upon the bell; / My mistress made it one upon my cheek. / She is so hot because the meat is cold; / The meat is cold because you come not home; / You come not home because you have no stomach; / You have no stomach, having broke your fast; / But we that know what 'tis to fast and pray, / Are penitent for your default today.

Back so soon? More like too late. The chicken's burning, the pig's falling off the spit, the clock has struck twelve, and my mistress has struck one on my cheek. She's hot because the food is cold; the food is cold because you haven't come home; you haven't come home because you're not hungry; you're not hungry because you've already eaten. But we who know what it is to fast and pray are being punished for your fault today.
Stop in your wind, sir, tell me this, I pray: / Where have you left the money that I gave you?
Hold your breath, sir, and tell me this, please: where have you left the money I gave you?
O, sixpence that I had o' Wednesday last / To pay the saddler for my mistress' crupper: / The saddler had it, sir, I kept it not.
Oh, the sixpence I had last Wednesday to pay the saddler for my mistress's crupper? The saddler had it, sir, I didn't keep it.
I am not in a sportive humour now. / Tell me, and dally not, where is the money? / We being strangers here, how dar'st thou trust / So great a charge from thine own custody?
I'm in no mood for jokes now. Tell me, and don't mess about: where is the money? We are strangers here, so how dare you let such a large sum out of your own keeping?

I pray you jest, sir, as you sit at dinner: / I from my mistress come to you in post; / If I return, I shall be post indeed, / For she will score your fault upon my pate. / Methinks your maw, like mine, should be your clock, / And strike you home without a messenger.

Please save your jokes till you're sitting at dinner. I've rushed here from my mistress. If I go back without you, I'll be a post indeed, for she'll chalk up your fault on my head. I'd have thought your stomach, like mine, would be your clock and send you home without a messenger.
Come, Dromio, come, these jests are out of season, / Reserve them till a merrier hour than this. / Where is the gold I gave in charge to thee?
Come on, Dromio, these jokes are out of place. Save them for a happier time. Where is the gold I left in your charge?
To me, sir? why, you gave no gold to me!
With me, sir? Why, you gave me no gold!
Come on, sir knave, have done your foolishness, / And tell me how thou hast dispos'd thy charge.
Come on, you rogue, stop this foolery, and tell me what you've done with what I gave you.
My charge was but to fetch you from the mart / Home to your house, the Phoenix, sir, to dinner. / My mistress and her sister stay for you.
My charge was only to fetch you from the market to your house, the Phoenix, sir, for dinner. My mistress and her sister are waiting for you.

Now, as I am a Christian, answer me / In what safe place you have bestow'd my money, / Or I shall break that merry sconce of yours / That stands on tricks when I am undispos'd; / Where is the thousand marks thou hadst of me?
As I am a Christian, tell me where you have put my money safely, or I'll crack that jolly head of yours that insists on jokes when I'm not in the mood. Where are the thousand marks you had from me?

I have some marks of yours upon my pate, / Some of my mistress' marks upon my shoulders, / But not a thousand marks between you both. / If I should pay your worship those again, / Perchance you will not bear them patiently.
I have some marks from you on my head and some marks from my mistress on my shoulders, but not a thousand marks between you. If I paid them back to you, maybe you wouldn't take it patiently.
Thy mistress' marks? what mistress, slave, hast thou?
Your mistress's marks? What mistress have you got, slave?
Your worship's wife, my mistress at the Phoenix; / She that doth fast till you come home to dinner, / And prays that you will hie you home to dinner.
Your worship's wife, my mistress at the Phoenix: the one who is fasting till you come home to dinner and begs you to hurry home to dinner.
What, wilt thou flout me thus unto my face, / Being forbid? There, take you that, sir knave.
What, will you mock me to my face like this, when I've told you not to? There, take that, you rogue.
What mean you, sir? for God's sake hold your hands. / Nay, an you will not, sir, I'll take my heels.
What are you doing, sir? For God's sake, keep your hands off! No? If you won't, I'm off.

Upon my life, by some device or other / The villain is o'er-raught of all my money. / They say this town is full of cozenage, / As nimble jugglers that deceive the eye, / Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind, / Soul-killing witches that deform the body, / Disguised cheaters, prating mountebanks, / And many such-like liberties of sin: / If it prove so, I will be gone the sooner. / I'll to the Centaur to go seek this slave. / I greatly fear my money is not safe.

Upon my life, by some trick or other the rascal has been cheated of all my money. They say this town is full of trickery: quick-handed conjurors who fool the eye, sorcerers working in the dark who change people's minds, soul-destroying witches who deform the body, cheats in disguise, chattering quacks, and many other kinds of licensed sin. If that's what's happened, I'll leave all the sooner. I'll go to the Centaur to look for this slave. I'm very afraid my money isn't safe.
Neither my husband nor the slave return'd / That in such haste I sent to seek his master? / Sure, Luciana, it is two o'clock.
Hasn't my husband come back, or the slave I sent in such a hurry to find his master? Surely, Luciana, it's two o'clock.

Perhaps some merchant hath invited him, / And from the mart he's somewhere gone to dinner. / Good sister, let us dine, and never fret; / A man is master of his liberty; / Time is their master, and when they see time, / They'll go or come. If so, be patient, sister.

Perhaps some merchant has invited him, and he's gone from the market to dinner somewhere. Dear sister, let's eat and stop fretting. A man is master of his own freedom. Only time is their master, and they come and go as they see fit. So be patient, sister.
Why should their liberty than ours be more?
Why should they have more freedom than we do?
Because their business still lies out o' door.
Because their business always lies outside the house.
Look when I serve him so, he takes it ill.
But when I treat him like that, he takes it badly.
O, know he is the bridle of your will.
Oh, you should know that he is the bridle on your will.
There's none but asses will be bridled so.
Only donkeys let themselves be bridled like that.

Why, headstrong liberty is lash'd with woe. / There's nothing situate under heaven's eye / But hath his bound in earth, in sea, in sky. / The beasts, the fishes, and the winged fowls / Are their males' subjects, and at their controls. / Man, more divine, the masters of all these, / Lord of the wide world and wild wat'ry seas, / Indued with intellectual sense and souls, / Of more pre-eminence than fish and fowls, / Are masters to their females, and their lords: / Then let your will attend on their accords.

Why, headstrong freedom is whipped with sorrow. There is nothing under heaven that doesn't have its limits, on earth, in the sea or in the sky. The animals, the fish and the birds are subject to their males and under their control. Men, who are closer to God and masters of all these, lords of the wide world and the wild seas, gifted with reason and souls and ranked above fish and birds, are masters of their women and their lords. So let your will wait on theirs.
This servitude makes you to keep unwed.
This idea of servitude is what keeps you unmarried.
Not this, but troubles of the marriage-bed.
Not that, but the troubles of the marriage bed.
But, were you wedded, you would bear some sway.
But if you were married, you'd want some power.
Ere I learn love, I'll practise to obey.
Before I learn to love, I'll practise obeying.
How if your husband start some other where?
What if your husband went off somewhere else?
Till he come home again, I would forbear.
I'd put up with it till he came home again.

Patience unmov'd! No marvel though she pause; / They can be meek that have no other cause. / A wretched soul bruis'd with adversity, / We bid be quiet when we hear it cry; / But were we burd'ned with like weight of pain, / As much, or more, we should ourselves complain: / So thou, that hast no unkind mate to grieve thee, / With urging helpless patience would relieve me: / But if thou live to see like right bereft, / This fool-begg'd patience in thee will be left.

Patience that has never been tested! No wonder she can be calm: people find it easy to be meek when they have no cause not to be. When we hear a poor soul bruised by hardship cry out, we tell it to be quiet; but if we carried the same weight of pain, we would complain as much, or more. So you, with no unkind husband to hurt you, would comfort me by urging a patience that doesn't help. But if you live to see yourself wronged the same way, this foolish patience of yours will be dropped.
Well, I will marry one day, but to try. / Here comes your man, now is your husband nigh.
Well, I'll marry one day, just to find out. Here comes your servant. Your husband must be near.
Say, is your tardy master now at hand?
Tell me, is your late master on his way?
Nay, he's at two hands with me, and that my two ears can witness.
No, he's been at war with me, at two hands, and both my ears can witness it.
Say, didst thou speak with him? know'st thou his mind?
Tell me, did you speak to him? Do you know what he intends?
Ay, ay, he told his mind upon mine ear. / Beshrew his hand, I scarce could understand it.
Yes, yes, he told me his mind on my ear. Curse his hand, I could hardly understand it.
Spake he so doubtfully thou couldst not feel his meaning?
Did he speak so unclearly you couldn't grasp his meaning?
Nay, he struck so plainly I could too well feel his blows; and withal / so doubtfully that I could scarce understand them.
No, he hit so plainly I could feel his blows all too well, and yet so confusingly that I could hardly make sense of them.
But say, I prithee, is he coming home? / It seems he hath great care to please his wife.
But tell me, please, is he coming home? He seems to care a great deal about pleasing his wife.
Why, mistress, sure my master is horn-mad.
Why, mistress, my master is certainly horn-mad.

I mean not cuckold-mad, / But sure he's stark mad. / When I desir'd him to come home to dinner, / He ask'd me for a thousand marks in gold. / "'Tis dinner time," quoth I. "My gold," quoth he. / "Your meat doth burn" quoth I. "My gold," quoth he. / "Will you come home?" quoth I. "My gold," quoth he. / "Where is the thousand marks I gave thee, villain?" / "The pig" quoth I "is burn'd". "My gold," quoth he. / "My mistress, sir," quoth I. "Hang up thy mistress; / I know not thy mistress; out on thy mistress!"

I don't mean mad like a man with a cheating wife, but he's certainly stark mad. When I asked him to come home to dinner, he asked me for a thousand marks in gold. "It's dinnertime," I said. "My gold," he said. "Your meat is burning," I said. "My gold," he said. "Will you come home?" I said. "My gold," he said. "Where are the thousand marks I gave you, villain?" "The pig is burnt," I said. "My gold," he said. "My mistress, sir," I said. "Hang your mistress! I don't know your mistress. To hell with your mistress!"

Quoth my master. / "I know," quoth he, "no house, no wife, no mistress." / So that my errand, due unto my tongue, / I thank him, I bare home upon my shoulders; / For, in conclusion, he did beat me there.

My master said it. "I know of no house, no wife, no mistress," he said. So the message that should have been carried home by my tongue, I carried home on my shoulders, thanks to him, because in the end he beat me there.
Go back again, thou slave, and fetch him home.
Go back again, you slave, and bring him home.
Go back again, and be new beaten home? / For God's sake, send some other messenger.
Go back again and be beaten home all over again? For God's sake, send some other messenger.
Back slave, or I will break thy pate across.
Go back, slave, or I'll crack your head across.
And he will bless that cross with other beating. / Between you I shall have a holy head.
And he'll bless that cross with more beating. Between the two of you I'll have a holy head.
Hence, prating peasant. Fetch thy master home.
Get out, you babbling peasant! Bring your master home.
Am I so round with you, as you with me, / That like a football you do spurn me thus? / You spurn me hence, and he will spurn me hither. / If I last in this service, you must case me in leather.

Am I so round with you, as you are with me, that you kick me about like a football? You kick me there and he kicks me back here. If I'm to last in this job, you'll have to stitch me up in leather like a ball.
Fie, how impatience loureth in your face.
Shame, how impatience scowls in your face!

His company must do his minions grace, / Whilst I at home starve for a merry look. / Hath homely age th' alluring beauty took / From my poor cheek? then he hath wasted it. / Are my discourses dull? barren my wit? / If voluble and sharp discourse be marr'd, / Unkindness blunts it more than marble hard. / Do their gay vestments his affections bait? / That's not my fault; he's master of my state. / What ruins are in me that can be found / By him not ruin'd? Then is he the ground / Of my defeatures. My decayed fair / A sunny look of his would soon repair; / But, too unruly deer, he breaks the pale / And feeds from home; poor I am but his stale.

His girlfriends must be enjoying his company, while I'm at home starving for one kind look from him. Has plain old age taken the attractive beauty from my poor cheek? Then he's the one who wasted it. Is my conversation dull, my wit barren? If my lively, sharp talk is spoilt, his unkindness has blunted it more than hard marble would. Do other women's bright clothes lure his affections? That isn't my fault: he controls my money. What ruins can be found in me that he hasn't ruined? So he is the cause of my lost looks. One sunny look from him would soon restore my faded beauty. But like a deer that won't be fenced in, he breaks out and feeds away from home, and poor I am only his laughing-stock.
Self-harming jealousy! fie, beat it hence.
Jealousy that only hurts yourself! For shame, drive it away.

Unfeeling fools can with such wrongs dispense. / I know his eye doth homage otherwhere, / Or else what lets it but he would be here? / Sister, you know he promis'd me a chain; / Would that alone, a love he would detain, / So he would keep fair quarter with his bed. / I see the jewel best enamelled / Will lose his beauty; yet the gold bides still / That others touch, yet often touching will / Wear gold; and no man that hath a name / By falsehood and corruption doth it shame. / Since that my beauty cannot please his eye, / I'll weep what's left away, and weeping die.

Only unfeeling fools could put up with such wrongs. I know his eye pays its respects somewhere else, or else what keeps him from being here? Sister, you know he promised me a chain. I'd give up that, the one gift he's holding back, if only he'd stay faithful to his marriage bed. I see that even the best enamelled jewel loses its beauty. The gold still lasts, though others handle it, but frequent handling will wear even gold away, and so any man with a good name is shamed by falsehood and corruption. Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep away what's left of it, and die weeping.
How many fond fools serve mad jealousy!
How many foolish people make themselves slaves to mad jealousy!

The gold I gave to Dromio is laid up / Safe at the Centaur, and the heedful slave / Is wander'd forth in care to seek me out. / By computation and mine host's report. / I could not speak with Dromio since at first / I sent him from the mart. See, here he comes.

The gold I gave Dromio is safely locked up at the Centaur, and the careful slave has wandered off to look for me. By my reckoning and the innkeeper's account, I couldn't have spoken to Dromio since I first sent him from the market. Look, here he comes.

How now, sir! is your merry humour alter'd? / As you love strokes, so jest with me again. / You know no Centaur? you receiv'd no gold? / Your mistress sent to have me home to dinner? / My house was at the Phoenix? Wast thou mad, / That thus so madly thou didst answer me?

Well, sir! Has your jolly mood changed? If you like being hit, joke with me again. You don't know the Centaur? You got no gold? Your mistress sent you to bring me home to dinner? My house was at the Phoenix? Were you mad, to answer me so madly?
What answer, sir? when spake I such a word?
What answer, sir? When did I say anything like that?
Even now, even here, not half an hour since.
Just now, right here, not half an hour ago.
I did not see you since you sent me hence, / Home to the Centaur with the gold you gave me.
I haven't seen you since you sent me off to the Centaur with the gold you gave me.
Villain, thou didst deny the gold's receipt, / And told'st me of a mistress and a dinner, / For which I hope thou felt'st I was displeas'd.
Villain, you denied getting the gold and told me about a mistress and a dinner, and I hope you felt how annoyed I was about it.
I am glad to see you in this merry vein. / What means this jest, I pray you, master, tell me?
I'm glad to see you in such a merry mood. What is this joke? Please tell me, master.
Yea, dost thou jeer and flout me in the teeth? / Think'st thou I jest? Hold, take thou that, and that.
What, are you mocking me to my face? Do you think I'm joking? There, take that, and that.
Hold, sir, for God's sake, now your jest is earnest. / Upon what bargain do you give it me?
Stop, sir, for God's sake! Now your joke's turned serious. What deal are you giving me this for?

Because that I familiarly sometimes / Do use you for my fool, and chat with you, / Your sauciness will jest upon my love, / And make a common of my serious hours. / When the sun shines let foolish gnats make sport, / But creep in crannies when he hides his beams. / If you will jest with me, know my aspect, / And fashion your demeanour to my looks, / Or I will beat this method in your sconce.

Because I sometimes treat you like a friend, use you as my fool and chat with you, your cheekiness takes advantage of my kindness and treats my serious moments as fair game. When the sun shines, foolish gnats can play, but they should creep into cracks when it hides its rays. If you want to joke with me, read my face and match your behaviour to my looks, or I'll beat that lesson into your sconce.

Sconce, call you it? so you would leave battering, I had rather have it / a head. And you use these blows long, I must get a sconce for my head, / and ensconce it too, or else I shall seek my wit in my shoulders. But I / pray, sir, why am I beaten?

Sconce, do you call it? If you'd stop battering it, I'd rather it was a head. If you keep up these blows much longer, I'll have to get a fort for my head and ensconce it too, or I'll be looking for my brains in my shoulders. But please, sir, why am I being beaten?
Nothing, sir, but that I am beaten.
Nothing, sir, except that I'm beaten.
Ay, sir, and wherefore; for they say, every why hath a wherefore.
Yes, sir, and wherefore, for they say every why has a wherefore.
Why, first, for flouting me; and then wherefore, / For urging it the second time to me.
Why, first, for mocking me; and then wherefore, for doing it a second time.
Was there ever any man thus beaten out of season, / When in the why and the wherefore is neither rhyme nor reason? / Well, sir, I thank you.
Was any man ever beaten so out of season, when there's neither rhyme nor reason in the why and the wherefore? Well, sir, thank you.
Marry, sir, for this something that you gave me for nothing.
Why, sir, for this something you gave me for nothing.
I'll make you amends next, to give you nothing for something. / But say, sir, is it dinner-time?
Next time I'll make it up to you by giving you nothing for something. But tell me, sir, is it dinnertime?
No, sir; I think the meat wants that I have.
No, sir. I think the meat lacks something I've had.
In good time, sir, what's that?
Well, sir, then it will be dry.
If it be, sir, I pray you eat none of it.
If it is, sir, please don't eat any of it.
Lest it make you choleric, and purchase me another dry basting.
In case it makes you angry and earns me another dry basting.
Well, sir, learn to jest in good time. / There's a time for all things.
Well, sir, learn to joke at the right time. There's a time for everything.
I durst have denied that before you were so choleric.
I'd have dared to deny that before you got so angry.
Marry, sir, by a rule as plain as the plain bald pate of Father Time / himself.
Why, sir, on grounds as plain as the plain bald head of Father Time himself.
There's no time for a man to recover his hair that grows bald by / nature.
There's no time for a man who goes bald naturally to get his hair back.
May he not do it by fine and recovery?
Can't he get it back by a legal fine and recovery?
Yes, to pay a fine for a periwig, and recover the lost hair of another / man.
Yes, by paying a fee for a wig and recovering the lost hair of another man.
Why is Time such a niggard of hair, being, as it is, so plentiful an / excrement?
Why is Time so stingy with hair, when it's something the body grows so plentifully?
Because it is a blessing that he bestows on beasts, and what he hath / scanted men in hair he hath given them in wit.
Because it's a blessing he gives to animals, and what he's skimped on giving men in hair he's given them in brains.
Why, but there's many a man hath more hair than wit.
Why, but there's many a man with more hair than brains.
Not a man of those but he hath the wit to lose his hair.
Every one of them has the brains to lose his hair.
Why, thou didst conclude hairy men plain dealers without wit.
Why, you've just concluded that hairy men are simple fellows without brains.
The plainer dealer, the sooner lost. Yet he loseth it in a kind of / jollity.
The simpler the fellow, the sooner he loses it. Still, he loses it while having a good time.
For two, and sound ones too.
For two, and sound ones too.
Nay, not sound, I pray you.
Nay, not sure, in a thing falsing.
No, not sure, in something so unreliable.
The one, to save the money that he spends in tiring; the other, that at / dinner they should not drop in his porridge.
One, to save the money he spends on hairdressing; the other, so that it doesn't drop into his soup at dinner.
You would all this time have proved there is no time for all things.
All this time you were trying to prove there isn't a time for everything.
Marry, and did, sir; namely, e'en no time to recover hair lost by / nature.
Yes, and I did, sir: namely, no time to recover hair lost naturally.
But your reason was not substantial why there is no time to recover.
But you didn't give a solid reason why there's no time to recover it.
Thus I mend it: Time himself is bald, and therefore, to the world's end / will have bald followers.
I'll put it right like this: Time himself is bald, so until the end of the world he'll have bald followers.
I knew 'twould be a bald conclusion. / But soft! who wafts us yonder?
I knew it would be a bald conclusion. But wait! Who's that waving to us over there?

Ay, ay, Antipholus, look strange and frown, / Some other mistress hath thy sweet aspects. / I am not Adriana, nor thy wife. / The time was once when thou unurg'd wouldst vow / That never words were music to thine ear, / That never object pleasing in thine eye, / That never touch well welcome to thy hand, / That never meat sweet-savour'd in thy taste, / Unless I spake, or look'd, or touch'd, or carv'd to thee. / How comes it now, my husband, O, how comes it, / That thou art then estranged from thyself? / Thyself I call it, being strange to me, / That, undividable, incorporate, / Am better than thy dear self's better part. / Ah, do not tear away thyself from me; / For know, my love, as easy mayst thou fall / A drop of water in the breaking gulf, / And take unmingled thence that drop again / Without addition or diminishing, / As take from me thyself, and not me too. / How dearly would it touch thee to the quick, / Should'st thou but hear I were licentious? / And that this body, consecrate to thee, / By ruffian lust should be contaminate? / Wouldst thou not spit at me, and spurn at me, / And hurl the name of husband in my face, / And tear the stain'd skin off my harlot brow, / And from my false hand cut the wedding-ring, / And break it with a deep-divorcing vow? / I know thou canst; and therefore, see thou do it. / I am possess'd with an adulterate blot; / My blood is mingled with the crime of lust; / For if we two be one, and thou play false, / I do digest the poison of thy flesh, / Being strumpeted by thy contagion. / Keep then fair league and truce with thy true bed, / I live distain'd, thou undishonoured.

Yes, yes, Antipholus, look like a stranger and frown. Some other mistress gets your sweet looks. I'm not Adriana, or your wife. There was a time when you'd swear without being asked that no words were music to your ear, no sight pleasing to your eye, no touch welcome to your hand, no food tasty to you, unless I spoke, or looked, or touched, or carved it for you. How is it now, my husband, oh, how is it that you're so estranged from yourself? I call it your self, since you're estranged from me, and I, who am inseparable from you, one body with you, am better than the better part of your own dear self. Ah, don't tear yourself away from me. Know this, my love: you might as easily let a drop of water fall into the breaking sea and take that same drop out again, unmixed, with nothing added or lost, as take yourself away from me without taking me too. How deeply it would wound you if you heard I was unfaithful, and that this body, dedicated to you, had been defiled by some thug's lust! Wouldn't you spit at me and kick me, throw the word "husband" in my face, tear the stained skin off my whore's forehead, cut the wedding ring off my false hand and break it with a vow of divorce? I know you could; so see that you do it. I am stained with adultery; my blood is mixed with the crime of lust. For if we two are one, and you are unfaithful, then I take in the poison of your flesh and am made a whore by your infection. So keep faith and peace with your true marriage bed; then I live unstained, and you undishonoured.

Plead you to me, fair dame? I know you not. / In Ephesus I am but two hours old, / As strange unto your town as to your talk, / Who, every word by all my wit being scann'd, / Wants wit in all one word to understand.

Are you pleading with me, lady? I don't know you. I've only been in Ephesus two hours, and I'm as much a stranger to your town as to your talk. I've examined every word with all my wits, and I can't understand a single one.
Fie, brother, how the world is chang'd with you. / When were you wont to use my sister thus? / She sent for you by Dromio home to dinner.
Shame, brother, how you've changed! When did you ever treat my sister like this? She sent Dromio to bring you home to dinner.
By thee; and this thou didst return from him, / That he did buffet thee, and in his blows / Denied my house for his, me for his wife.
You. And this is the answer you brought back from him: that he hit you, and with his blows denied my house was his and I was his wife.
Did you converse, sir, with this gentlewoman? / What is the course and drift of your compact?
Have you talked with this lady, sir? What's the point and purpose of your plot?
I, sir? I never saw her till this time.
Me, sir? I never saw her before now.
Villain, thou liest, for even her very words / Didst thou deliver to me on the mart.
Villain, you're lying. You gave me her very words at the market.
I never spake with her in all my life.
I've never spoken to her in all my life.
How can she thus, then, call us by our names? / Unless it be by inspiration.
Then how can she call us by our names, unless by divine inspiration?

How ill agrees it with your gravity / To counterfeit thus grossly with your slave, / Abetting him to thwart me in my mood; / Be it my wrong, you are from me exempt, / But wrong not that wrong with a more contempt. / Come, I will fasten on this sleeve of thine. / Thou art an elm, my husband, I a vine, / Whose weakness, married to thy stronger state, / Makes me with thy strength to communicate: / If aught possess thee from me, it is dross, / Usurping ivy, brier, or idle moss, / Who all, for want of pruning, with intrusion / Infect thy sap, and live on thy confusion.

How badly it suits your dignity to put on such a crude act with your slave, egging him on to provoke me when I'm upset! It's wrong enough that you stay away from me; don't add insult to that injury. Come, I'll hold on to your sleeve. You are an elm, my husband, and I a vine: married to your strength, my weakness shares in it. If anything takes you from me, it's rubbish: parasitic ivy, briars or useless moss that, for lack of pruning, creep in, poison your sap and live off your ruin.

To me she speaks; she moves me for her theme. / What, was I married to her in my dream? / Or sleep I now, and think I hear all this? / What error drives our eyes and ears amiss? / Until I know this sure uncertainty / I'll entertain the offer'd fallacy.

She's talking to me; I'm her subject. What, did I marry her in a dream? Or am I asleep now and only think I hear all this? What error is leading our eyes and ears astray? Until I'm sure what this uncertainty is, I'll go along with the illusion on offer.
Dromio, go bid the servants spread for dinner.
Dromio, go and tell the servants to lay the table for dinner.

O, for my beads! I cross me for a sinner. / This is the fairy land; O spite of spites! / We talk with goblins, owls, and sprites; / If we obey them not, this will ensue: / They'll suck our breath, or pinch us black and blue.

Oh, for my rosary! I cross myself, sinner that I am. This is fairyland. Oh, worst of all! We're talking to goblins, owls and spirits. If we don't obey them, this is what will happen: they'll suck the breath out of us, or pinch us black and blue.
Why prat'st thou to thyself, and answer'st not? / Dromio, thou drone, thou snail, thou slug, thou sot.
Why are you muttering to yourself and not answering? Dromio, you drone, you snail, you slug, you idiot!
I am transformed, master, am I not?
I've been transformed, master, haven't I?
I think thou art in mind, and so am I.
I think you have in your mind, and so have I.
Nay, master, both in mind and in my shape.
No, master, in my mind and in my body.
You still have your own shape.
If thou art chang'd to aught, 'tis to an ass.
If you've been changed into anything, it's a donkey.
'Tis true; she rides me, and I long for grass. / 'Tis so, I am an ass; else it could never be / But I should know her as well as she knows me.
That's true: she rides me and I long for grass. That's it, I'm a donkey; otherwise I would surely know her as well as she knows me.

Come, come, no longer will I be a fool, / To put the finger in the eye and weep / Whilst man and master laughs my woes to scorn. / Come, sir, to dinner; Dromio, keep the gate. / Husband, I'll dine above with you today, / And shrive you of a thousand idle pranks. / Sirrah, if any ask you for your master, / Say he dines forth, and let no creature enter. / Come, sister; Dromio, play the porter well.

Come, come, I won't be a fool any longer, rubbing my eyes and crying while servant and master laugh at my sorrows. Come, sir, to dinner. Dromio, guard the gate. Husband, I'll dine upstairs with you today and make you confess a thousand silly tricks. Fellow, if anyone asks for your master, say he's dining out, and let nobody in. Come, sister. Dromio, be a good porter.

Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell? / Sleeping or waking, mad, or well-advis'd? / Known unto these, and to myself disguis'd! / I'll say as they say, and persever so, / And in this mist at all adventures go.

Am I on earth, in heaven or in hell? Asleep or awake, mad or in my right mind? Known to these people, and a mystery to myself! I'll say what they say and stick to it, and go wherever this fog takes me.
Master, shall I be porter at the gate?
Master, shall I be porter at the gate?
Ay; and let none enter, lest I break your pate.
Yes, and let no one in, or I'll break your head.
Come, come, Antipholus, we dine too late.
Come on, Antipholus, we're late for dinner.

Good Signior Angelo, you must excuse us all, / My wife is shrewish when I keep not hours. / Say that I linger'd with you at your shop / To see the making of her carcanet, / And that tomorrow you will bring it home. / But here's a villain that would face me down. / He met me on the mart, and that I beat him, / And charg'd him with a thousand marks in gold, / And that I did deny my wife and house. / Thou drunkard, thou, what didst thou mean by this?

Good Signor Angelo, you must make excuses for all of us. My wife gets sharp-tongued when I'm late. Say I stayed with you at your shop to watch her necklace being made, and that you'll bring it to the house tomorrow. But here's a rascal who'd insist to my face that he met me at the market, that I beat him and demanded a thousand marks in gold from him, and that I denied having a wife and a house. You drunkard, what did you mean by this?

Say what you will, sir, but I know what I know. / That you beat me at the mart I have your hand to show; / If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink, / Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.

Say what you like, sir, I know what I know. That you beat me at the market I've got your handwriting to prove. If my skin were parchment and your blows were ink, your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
I think thou art an ass.
Marry, so it doth appear / By the wrongs I suffer and the blows I bear. / I should kick, being kick'd; and being at that pass, / You would keep from my heels, and beware of an ass.
Yes, it looks that way, from the wrongs I suffer and the blows I take. Being kicked, I ought to kick back, and if I did, you'd keep away from my heels and beware of a donkey.
You're sad, Signior Balthasar; pray God our cheer / May answer my good will and your good welcome here.
You're very serious, Signor Balthasar. I pray to God our food lives up to my goodwill and your welcome here.
I hold your dainties cheap, sir, and your welcome dear.
I value your food lightly, sir, and your welcome highly.
O, Signior Balthasar, either at flesh or fish / A table full of welcome makes scarce one dainty dish.
Oh, Signor Balthasar, whether it's meat or fish, a whole table of welcome hardly makes one tasty dish.
Good meat, sir, is common; that every churl affords.
Good food is common, sir; any peasant can provide it.
And welcome more common, for that's nothing but words.
And a welcome is more common, because that's nothing but words.
Small cheer and great welcome makes a merry feast.
Plain food and a warm welcome make a happy feast.

Ay, to a niggardly host and more sparing guest. / But though my cates be mean, take them in good part; / Better cheer may you have, but not with better heart. / But soft; my door is lock'd. Go bid them let us in.

Yes, for a stingy host and a guest who eats even less. But though my food is plain, take it in good spirit. You might get better food elsewhere, but not served more warmly. But wait, my door's locked. Go and tell them to let us in.
Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cicely, Gillian, Ginn!
Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cicely, Gillian, Ginn!

[Within] Mome, malt-horse, capon, coxcomb, idiot, patch! / Either get thee from the door or sit down at the hatch: / Dost thou conjure for wenches, that thou call'st for such store / When one is one too many? Go, get thee from the door.

Dope, carthorse, capon, coxcomb, idiot, fool! Either get away from the door or sit down at the half-door. Are you casting spells for girls, calling for so many, when one is one too many? Go on, get away from the door.
What patch is made our porter? My master stays in the street.
What fool has been made our porter? My master's waiting in the street.
Let him walk from whence he came, lest he catch cold on's feet.
Let him walk back where he came from, or he'll catch cold in his feet.
Who talks within there? Ho, open the door.
Who's that talking inside? Hey, open the door!
Right, sir, I'll tell you when an you'll tell me wherefore.
All right, sir, I'll tell you when, if you'll tell me why.
Wherefore? For my dinner. I have not dined today.
Why? For my dinner. I haven't eaten today.
Nor today here you must not; come again when you may.
And you won't today, not here. Come back when you can.
What art thou that keep'st me out from the house I owe?
Who are you, keeping me out of the house I own?
The porter for this time, sir, and my name is Dromio.
The porter for now, sir, and my name is Dromio.

O villain, thou hast stolen both mine office and my name; / The one ne'er got me credit, the other mickle blame. / If thou hadst been Dromio today in my place, / Thou wouldst have chang'd thy face for a name, or thy name for an ass.

Oh, you villain, you've stolen both my job and my name! One never earned me any credit, the other plenty of blame. If you'd been Dromio in my place today, you'd have swapped your face for another name, or your name for a donkey's.
[Within] What a coil is there, Dromio, who are those at the gate?
What's all this racket, Dromio? Who's that at the gate?
Faith, no, he comes too late, / And so tell your master.
Honestly, no. He's come too late, and you can tell your master so.
O Lord, I must laugh; / Have at you with a proverb:—Shall I set in my staff?
Oh Lord, I have to laugh. Here's a proverb for you: shall I plant my staff and settle in?
Have at you with another: that's—When? can you tell?
Here's another for you: that's "When? Can you tell me?"
If thy name be called Luce,—Luce, thou hast answer'd him well.
If your name is Luce, then Luce, you've answered him well.
Do you hear, you minion? you'll let us in, I hope?
Do you hear, you hussy? You'll let us in, I hope?
I thought to have ask'd you.
I meant to ask you that.
So, come, help. Well struck, there was blow for blow.
So, come on, help. Well struck! That was blow for blow.
Can you tell for whose sake?
Can you tell me for whose sake I should?
Master, knock hard on the door.
Let him knock till it ache.
Let him knock till his hand aches.
You'll cry for this, minion, if I beat the door down.
You'll be sorry for this, hussy, if I beat the door down.
What needs all that, and a pair of stocks in the town?
Why do that, when there's a pair of stocks in town for you?
[Within] Who is that at the door that keeps all this noise?
Who's that at the door making all this noise?
By my troth, your town is troubled with unruly boys.
Honestly, your town is plagued with rowdy boys.
Are you there, wife? you might have come before.
Is that you, wife? You might have come sooner.
Your wife, sir knave? go, get you from the door.
Your wife, you rogue? Go on, get away from the door.
If you went in pain, master, this knave would go sore.
If you went in pain, master, this rogue would go sore.
Here is neither cheer, sir, nor welcome. We would fain have either.
There's neither food nor welcome here, sir. We'd gladly have either.
In debating which was best, we shall part with neither.
While we were arguing about which was best, we've ended up with neither.
They stand at the door, master; bid them welcome hither.
They're standing at the door, master. Tell them they're welcome here.
There is something in the wind, that we cannot get in.
Something's in the wind, that we can't get in.
You would say so, master, if your garments were thin. / Your cake here is warm within; you stand here in the cold. / It would make a man mad as a buck to be so bought and sold.
You'd say so, master, if your clothes were thin. Your cake's warm inside, while you stand here in the cold. It would make a man mad as a buck to be tricked and betrayed like this.
Go, fetch me something, I'll break ope the gate.
Go and fetch me something. I'll break the gate open.
Break any breaking here, and I'll break your knave's pate.
Break anything here, and I'll break your rogue's head.
A man may break a word with you, sir, and words are but wind; / Ay, and break it in your face, so he break it not behind.
A man may break a word with you, sir, since words are only wind; yes, and break it in your face, as long as he doesn't break wind behind.
It seems thou want'st breaking; out upon thee, hind!
Looks like you need breaking. Get away, you peasant!
Here's too much "out upon thee"; I pray thee, let me in.
There's too much "get away" here. Please, let me in.
Ay, when fowls have no feathers and fish have no fin.
Yes, when birds have no feathers and fish have no fins.
Well, I'll break in; go, borrow me a crow.
Well, I'll break in. Go and borrow me a crowbar.
A crow without feather; master, mean you so? / For a fish without a fin, there's a fowl without a feather. / If a crow help us in, sirrah, we'll pluck a crow together.
A crow without feathers, master, is that what you mean? For a fish without a fin, here's a bird without a feather. If a crow helps us get in, fellow, we'll have a crow to pluck together.
Go, get thee gone; fetch me an iron crow.
Go on, get going. Fetch me an iron crowbar.

Have patience, sir. O, let it not be so: / Herein you war against your reputation, / And draw within the compass of suspect / The unviolated honour of your wife. / Once this,—your long experience of her wisdom, / Her sober virtue, years, and modesty, / Plead on her part some cause to you unknown; / And doubt not, sir, but she will well excuse / Why at this time the doors are made against you. / Be rul'd by me; depart in patience, / And let us to the Tiger all to dinner, / And about evening, come yourself alone / To know the reason of this strange restraint. / If by strong hand you offer to break in / Now in the stirring passage of the day, / A vulgar comment will be made of it; / And that supposed by the common rout / Against your yet ungalled estimation / That may with foul intrusion enter in, / And dwell upon your grave when you are dead; / For slander lives upon succession, / For ever hous'd where it gets possession.

Be patient, sir. Oh, don't do this! You'd be fighting against your own good name and bringing your wife's spotless honour under suspicion. Consider this: your long experience of her good sense, her steady virtue, her maturity and modesty suggest she has some reason you don't know about. Don't doubt, sir, that she'll explain why the doors are shut against you right now. Take my advice: leave calmly, and let's all go to the Tiger for dinner. Then towards evening come back on your own to find out the reason for this strange lockout. If you try to break in by force now, at the busiest time of day, people will gossip about it, and the common crowd will make up some story against your reputation, which is still unspoiled. That story could worm its way in and linger over your grave when you are dead. For slander passes from one generation to the next, and lives for ever wherever it takes hold.

You have prevail'd. I will depart in quiet, / And, in despite of mirth, mean to be merry. / I know a wench of excellent discourse, / Pretty and witty; wild, and yet, too, gentle; / There will we dine. This woman that I mean, / My wife (but, I protest, without desert) / Hath oftentimes upbraided me withal; / To her will we to dinner.—Get you home / And fetch the chain, by this I know 'tis made. / Bring it, I pray you, to the Porpentine, / For there's the house. That chain will I bestow / (Be it for nothing but to spite my wife) / Upon mine hostess there. Good sir, make haste. / Since mine own doors refuse to entertain me, / I'll knock elsewhere, to see if they'll disdain me.

You've won. I'll leave quietly and, though I'm in no mood for fun, I mean to be merry. I know a woman who's an excellent talker, pretty and witty, lively and yet gentle too. We'll eat there. My wife has often nagged me about this woman, though I swear without reason. We'll go to her for dinner. (To Angelo) Go home and fetch the chain; I know it must be made by now. Please bring it to the Porcupine, because that's the house. I'll give that chain to the hostess there, if only to spite my wife. Hurry, good sir. Since my own doors refuse to welcome me, I'll knock somewhere else and see if they'll turn me away.
I'll meet you at that place some hour hence.
I'll meet you there in about an hour.
Do so; this jest shall cost me some expense.
Do. This joke will cost me something.

And may it be that you have quite forgot / A husband's office? Shall, Antipholus, / Even in the spring of love, thy love-springs rot? / Shall love, in building, grow so ruinous? / If you did wed my sister for her wealth, / Then for her wealth's sake use her with more kindness; / Or if you like elsewhere, do it by stealth, / Muffle your false love with some show of blindness. / Let not my sister read it in your eye; / Be not thy tongue thy own shame's orator; / Look sweet, speak fair, become disloyalty; / Apparel vice like virtue's harbinger; / Bear a fair presence though your heart be tainted; / Teach sin the carriage of a holy saint, / Be secret-false. What need she be acquainted? / What simple thief brags of his own attaint? / 'Tis double wrong to truant with your bed / And let her read it in thy looks at board. / Shame hath a bastard fame, well managed; / Ill deeds is doubled with an evil word. / Alas, poor women, make us but believe, / Being compact of credit, that you love us. / Though others have the arm, show us the sleeve; / We in your motion turn, and you may move us. / Then, gentle brother, get you in again; / Comfort my sister, cheer her, call her wife. / 'Tis holy sport to be a little vain / When the sweet breath of flattery conquers strife.

Can it really be that you have completely forgotten a husband's duty? Antipholus, will your love's young shoots rot in the very spring of love? Will love fall into ruins while it's still being built? If you married my sister for her money, then for her money's sake treat her more kindly. Or if you love someone else, do it in secret: hide your false love behind some sort of blindfold. Don't let my sister read it in your eyes; don't let your tongue announce your own shame. Look sweet, speak kindly, make disloyalty look good; dress vice up as if it came before virtue. Look decent even if your heart is tainted. Teach sin to behave like a holy saint. Be false in secret. Why does she need to know? What foolish thief boasts about his own crime? It's doubly wrong to be unfaithful to your bed and let her read it in your face at the table. Shame, if handled well, can pass for a kind of good name; bad deeds are made twice as bad by bad words. Alas, poor women! Since we are made to trust, just let us believe you love us. Even if others get your arm, let us have the sleeve. We turn as you move; you can sway us. So, gentle brother, go back inside. Comfort my sister, cheer her up, call her your wife. It's a holy game to tell a few white lies when sweet flattery puts an end to quarrelling.

Sweet mistress, what your name is else, I know not, / Nor by what wonder you do hit on mine; / Less in your knowledge and your grace you show not / Than our earth's wonder, more than earth divine. / Teach me, dear creature, how to think and speak; / Lay open to my earthy gross conceit, / Smother'd in errors, feeble, shallow, weak, / The folded meaning of your words' deceit. / Against my soul's pure truth why labour you / To make it wander in an unknown field? / Are you a god? would you create me new? / Transform me, then, and to your power I'll yield. / But if that I am I, then well I know / Your weeping sister is no wife of mine, / Nor to her bed no homage do I owe. / Far more, far more, to you do I decline. / O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note / To drown me in thy sister's flood of tears. / Sing, siren, for thyself, and I will dote; / Spread o'er the silver waves thy golden hairs, / And as a bed I'll take thee, and there lie, / And, in that glorious supposition think / He gains by death that hath such means to die. / Let love, being light, be drowned if she sink!

Sweet lady, I don't know what your name is, nor by what miracle you know mine. Your knowledge and grace make you nothing less than a wonder of this earth, more divine than earthly. Teach me, dear creature, how to think and speak. Explain to my dull, earthly mind, lost in errors, feeble, shallow and weak, the hidden meaning of your puzzling words. Why are you trying to make my soul's plain truth wander off into unknown territory? Are you a goddess? Would you make me into someone new? Then transform me, and I'll give in to your power. But if I am who I am, then I know very well that your weeping sister is no wife of mine, and I owe her bed no loyalty. Far more, far more, I'm drawn to you. Oh, don't lure me with your song, sweet mermaid, to drown me in your sister's flood of tears. Sing for yourself, siren, and I'll adore you. Spread your golden hair over the silver waves, and I'll take it for my bed and lie there, and in that glorious dream think that a man who can die like that gains by dying. Let love, which is light, drown if it sinks!
What, are you mad, that you do reason so?
What, are you mad, to talk like this?
Not mad, but mated; how, I do not know.
Not mad, but bewildered; how, I don't know.
It is a fault that springeth from your eye.
The fault comes from your eye.
For gazing on your beams, fair sun, being by.
From gazing at your rays, lovely sun, so close by.
Gaze where you should, and that will clear your sight.
Look where you should look, and that will clear your sight.
As good to wink, sweet love, as look on night.
I might as well close my eyes, sweet love, as look at night.
Why call you me love? Call my sister so.
Why do you call me love? Call my sister that.

No, / It is thyself, mine own self's better part, / Mine eye's clear eye, my dear heart's dearer heart, / My food, my fortune, and my sweet hope's aim, / My sole earth's heaven, and my heaven's claim.
No, it's you: the better part of my own self, my eye's clear eye, my dear heart's dearer heart, my food, my fortune, the target of my sweet hope, my only heaven on earth and my claim on heaven.
All this my sister is, or else should be.
My sister is all this, or should be.
Call thyself sister, sweet, for I aim thee; / Thee will I love, and with thee lead my life; / Thou hast no husband yet, nor I no wife. / Give me thy hand.
Call yourself sister, sweetheart, for I'm aiming at you. I'll love you and spend my life with you. You don't have a husband yet, and I don't have a wife. Give me your hand.
O, soft, sir, hold you still; / I'll fetch my sister to get her goodwill.
Oh, wait, sir, stay where you are. I'll fetch my sister to get her blessing.
Why, how now, Dromio? where runn'st thou so fast?
Why, what's the matter, Dromio? Where are you running so fast?
Do you know me, sir? Am I Dromio? Am I your man? Am I myself?
Do you know me, sir? Am I Dromio? Am I your servant? Am I myself?
Thou art Dromio, thou art my man, thou art thyself.
You're Dromio, you're my servant, you're yourself.
I am an ass, I am a woman's man, and besides myself.
I'm a donkey, I'm a woman's man, and I'm beside myself.
What woman's man? and how besides thyself?
What woman's man? And how are you beside yourself?
Marry, sir, besides myself, I am due to a woman, one that claims me, / one that haunts me, one that will have me.
Why, sir, besides being myself, I belong to a woman: one who claims me, one who haunts me, one who will have me.
What claim lays she to thee?
What claim does she have on you?
Marry, sir, such claim as you would lay to your horse, and she would / have me as a beast; not that I being a beast she would have me, but / that she being a very beastly creature lays claim to me.
Why, sir, the sort of claim you'd make on your horse. She wants me as a beast: not that she'd want me because I'm a beast, but because she's such a beastly creature she lays claim to me.
A very reverent body; ay, such a one as a man may not speak of without / he say "sir-reverence". I have but lean luck in the match, and yet is / she a wondrous fat marriage.
A very reverend body; yes, the kind of person you can't mention without saying "excuse me". I have lean luck in the match, and yet it's an amazingly fat marriage.
How dost thou mean a "fat marriage"?
What do you mean, a "fat marriage"?

Marry, sir, she's the kitchen wench, and all grease, and I know not / what use to put her to but to make a lamp of her and run from her by / her own light. I warrant her rags and the tallow in them will burn a / Poland winter. If she lives till doomsday, she'll burn a week longer / than the whole world.

Why, sir, she's the kitchen maid, and all grease, and I don't know what use to make of her except turn her into a lamp and run away from her by her own light. I swear her rags and the fat in them would burn through a Polish winter. If she lives till Judgement Day, she'll burn a week longer than the whole world.
Swart like my shoe, but her face nothing like so clean kept. For why? / she sweats, a man may go overshoes in the grime of it.
Black as my shoe, but her face isn't kept anything like as clean. Why? Because she sweats so much a man could sink in the dirt over his shoes.
That's a fault that water will mend.
That's a fault water can fix.
No, sir, 'tis in grain; Noah's flood could not do it.
No, sir, it's dyed in. Noah's flood couldn't wash it out.
Nell, sir; but her name and three quarters, that's an ell and three / quarters, will not measure her from hip to hip.
Nell, sir. But her name and three quarters, that's an ell and three quarters, wouldn't measure her from hip to hip.
No longer from head to foot than from hip to hip. She is spherical, / like a globe. I could find out countries in her.
She's no longer from head to foot than from hip to hip. She's round, like a globe. I could find countries on her.
In what part of her body stands Ireland?
Where on her body is Ireland?
Marry, sir, in her buttocks; I found it out by the bogs.
Why, sir, in her buttocks: I found it by the bogs.
I found it by the barrenness, hard in the palm of the hand.
I found it by the barren ground, hard in the palm of her hand.
In her forehead; armed and reverted, making war against her hair.
In her forehead, armed and rebelling, making war against her hair.
I looked for the chalky cliffs, but I could find no whiteness in them. / But I guess it stood in her chin, by the salt rheum that ran between / France and it.
I looked for the chalk cliffs, but I couldn't find anything white about her. But I guess it was in her chin, from the salty snot that ran between France and it.
Faith, I saw it not; but I felt it hot in her breath.
Honestly, I didn't see it, but I felt it hot on her breath.
Where are America and the Indies?

O, sir, upon her nose, all o'er-embellished with rubies, carbuncles, / sapphires, declining their rich aspect to the hot breath of Spain, who / sent whole armadoes of carracks to be ballast at her nose.
Oh, sir, on her nose, all decorated with rubies, carbuncles and sapphires, turning their rich faces towards the hot breath of Spain, which sent whole fleets of galleons to be loaded up at her nose.
Where were Belgium and the Netherlands?

O, sir, I did not look so low. To conclude: this drudge or diviner laid / claim to me, called me Dromio, swore I was assured to her, told me what / privy marks I had about me, as the mark of my shoulder, the mole in my / neck, the great wart on my left arm, that I, amazed, ran from her as a / witch. And, I think, if my breast had not been made of faith, and my / heart of steel, she had transformed me to a curtal dog, and made me / turn i' the wheel.

Oh, sir, I didn't look that low. To sum up: this drudge, or witch, claimed me, called me Dromio, swore I was engaged to her, told me what private marks I had on me, like the mark on my shoulder, the mole on my neck, the big wart on my left arm, so that I was amazed and ran from her as from a witch. And I think if my breast hadn't been made of faith and my heart of steel, she'd have turned me into a dog with a docked tail and made me run in the turnspit wheel.

Go, hie thee presently, post to the road; / And if the wind blow any way from shore, / I will not harbour in this town tonight. / If any bark put forth, come to the mart, / Where I will walk till thou return to me. / If everyone knows us, and we know none, / 'Tis time, I think, to trudge, pack and be gone.

Go, hurry straight to the harbour. If the wind is blowing in any direction away from the shore, I won't stay in this town tonight. If any ship is sailing, come to the market, where I'll walk about till you come back to me. If everyone knows us and we know no one, it's time, I think, to pack up and go.
As from a bear a man would run for life, / So fly I from her that would be my wife.
As a man would run for his life from a bear, so I fly from the woman who'd be my wife.

There's none but witches do inhabit here, / And therefore 'tis high time that I were hence. / She that doth call me husband, even my soul / Doth for a wife abhor. But her fair sister, / Possess'd with such a gentle sovereign grace, / Of such enchanting presence and discourse, / Hath almost made me traitor to myself. / But lest myself be guilty to self-wrong, / I'll stop mine ears against the mermaid's song.

Only witches live here, so it's high time I left. My very soul hates the woman who calls me husband, as a wife. But her lovely sister, with such gentle, commanding grace and such enchanting looks and talk, has almost made me a traitor to myself. But so that I'm not guilty of wronging myself, I'll block my ears against the mermaid's song.
I know it well, sir. Lo, here is the chain; / I thought to have ta'en you at the Porpentine, / The chain unfinish'd made me stay thus long.
I know it well, sir. Look, here's the chain. I meant to catch you at the Porcupine, but the chain wasn't finished, and that kept me so long.
What is your will that I shall do with this?
What do you want me to do with this?
What please yourself, sir; I have made it for you.
Whatever you like, sir. I made it for you.
Made it for me, sir! I bespoke it not.
Made it for me, sir! I didn't order it.
Not once, nor twice, but twenty times you have. / Go home with it, and please your wife withal, / And soon at supper-time I'll visit you, / And then receive my money for the chain.
Not once or twice but twenty times you have. Take it home and please your wife with it, and soon, at suppertime, I'll call on you and get my money for the chain.
I pray you, sir, receive the money now, / For fear you ne'er see chain nor money more.
Please, sir, take the money now, in case you never see the chain or the money again.
You are a merry man, sir; fare you well.

What I should think of this I cannot tell, / But this I think, there's no man is so vain / That would refuse so fair an offer'd chain. / I see a man here needs not live by shifts, / When in the streets he meets such golden gifts. / I'll to the mart, and there for Dromio stay; / If any ship put out, then straight away.

I can't tell what to make of this. But I do think there's no man so foolish that he'd refuse such a fine chain when it's offered. I see a man here doesn't need to live by his wits when he meets such golden gifts in the street. I'll go to the market and wait there for Dromio. If any ship is sailing, we're off at once.

You know since Pentecost the sum is due, / And since I have not much importun'd you, / Nor now I had not, but that I am bound / To Persia, and want guilders for my voyage; / Therefore make present satisfaction, / Or I'll attach you by this officer.

You know the sum has been due since Whitsun, and I haven't pressed you much, and I wouldn't now, except that I'm bound for Persia and need money for my voyage. So pay me now, or I'll have this officer arrest you.

Even just the sum that I do owe to you / Is growing to me by Antipholus, / And in the instant that I met with you / He had of me a chain; at five o'clock / I shall receive the money for the same. / Pleaseth you walk with me down to his house, / I will discharge my bond, and thank you too.

The exact sum I owe you is owed to me by Antipholus. Just before I met you, he had a chain from me. At five o'clock I'll get the money for it. If you'll walk with me to his house, I'll pay off my debt, and thank you too.
That labour may you save. See where he comes.
You can save yourself the trouble. Look, here he comes.

While I go to the goldsmith's house, go thou / And buy a rope's end; that will I bestow / Among my wife and her confederates / For locking me out of my doors by day. / But soft, I see the goldsmith; get thee gone; / Buy thou a rope, and bring it home to me.

While I go to the goldsmith's house, you go and buy a rope's end. I'll use it on my wife and her accomplices for locking me out of my own house in broad daylight. But wait, I see the goldsmith. Off you go, buy a rope and bring it home to me.
I buy a thousand pound a year! I buy a rope!
I buy a thousand pounds a year! I buy a rope!

A man is well holp up that trusts to you, / I promised your presence and the chain, / But neither chain nor goldsmith came to me. / Belike you thought our love would last too long / If it were chain'd together, and therefore came not.

A man who trusts you gets a lot of help! I promised your company and the chain, but neither the chain nor the goldsmith turned up. I suppose you thought our love would last too long if it was chained together, so you didn't come.

Saving your merry humour, here's the note / How much your chain weighs to the utmost carat, / The fineness of the gold, and chargeful fashion, / Which doth amount to three odd ducats more / Than I stand debted to this gentleman. / I pray you, see him presently discharg'd, / For he is bound to sea, and stays but for it.

Joking aside, here's the bill: how much your chain weighs to the last carat, the fineness of the gold and the costly workmanship. It comes to three ducats or so more than I owe this gentleman. Please pay him straight away, because he's about to go to sea and is only waiting for this.

I am not furnished with the present money; / Besides, I have some business in the town. / Good signior, take the stranger to my house, / And with you take the chain, and bid my wife / Disburse the sum on the receipt thereof; / Perchance I will be there as soon as you.
