I don't have the cash on me, and besides, I have some business in town. Good signor, take the stranger to my house, take the chain with you, and tell my wife to pay the sum when she receives it. Maybe I'll be there as soon as you.
Then you will bring the chain to her yourself.
Then you'll bring the chain to her yourself?
No, bear it with you, lest I come not time enough.
No, take it with you, in case I'm not there in time.
Well, sir, I will. Have you the chain about you?
Well, sir, I will. Do you have the chain on you?
And if I have not, sir, I hope you have, / Or else you may return without your money.
If I haven't, sir, I hope you have, or else you may go back without your money.
Nay, come, I pray you, sir, give me the chain; / Both wind and tide stays for this gentleman, / And I, to blame, have held him here too long.
No, come on, sir, please give me the chain. Both wind and tide are waiting for this gentleman, and it's my fault I've kept him here so long.
Good Lord, you use this dalliance to excuse / Your breach of promise to the Porpentine. / I should have chid you for not bringing it, / But, like a shrew, you first begin to brawl.
Good Lord, you're using this nonsense to excuse breaking your promise to come to the Porcupine. I should have scolded you for not bringing it, but like a nagging wife you start the quarrel first.
The hour steals on; I pray you, sir, dispatch.
Time's passing. Please, sir, settle this.
You hear how he importunes me. The chain!
You hear how he's pressing me. The chain!
Why, give it to my wife, and fetch your money.
Why, give it to my wife and collect your money.
Come, come, you know I gave it you even now. / Either send the chain or send by me some token.
Come, come, you know I gave it to you just now. Either send the chain or send some token of authority with me.
Fie, now you run this humour out of breath. / Come, where's the chain? I pray you, let me see it.
Oh, now you're running this joke into the ground. Come on, where's the chain? Please, let me see it.
My business cannot brook this dalliance. / Good sir, say whe'er you'll answer me or no; / If not, I'll leave him to the officer.
My business can't put up with this time-wasting. Good sir, say whether you'll pay me or not. If not, I'll hand him over to the officer.
I answer you? What should I answer you?
I pay you? What should I pay you?
The money that you owe me for the chain.
The money you owe me for the chain.
I owe you none till I receive the chain.
I owe you nothing till I get the chain.
You know I gave it you half an hour since.
You know I gave it to you half an hour ago.
You gave me none. You wrong me much to say so.
You gave me nothing. You do me great wrong by saying so.
You wrong me more, sir, in denying it. / Consider how it stands upon my credit.
You do me more wrong, sir, by denying it. Think how my credit depends on it.
Well, officer, arrest him at my suit.
Well, officer, arrest him on my claim.
I do, and charge you in the duke's name to obey me.
I do, and order you in the Duke's name to obey me.
This touches me in reputation. / Either consent to pay this sum for me, / Or I attach you by this officer.
This threatens my reputation. Either agree to pay this sum for me, or I'll have this officer arrest you.
Consent to pay thee that I never had? / Arrest me, foolish fellow, if thou dar'st.
Agree to pay you for something I never had? Arrest me, you fool, if you dare.
Here is thy fee; arrest him, officer. / I would not spare my brother in this case / If he should scorn me so apparently.
Here's your fee. Arrest him, officer. I wouldn't spare my own brother in this situation if he scorned me so openly.
I do arrest you, sir. You hear the suit.
I arrest you, sir. You've heard the charge.
I do obey thee till I give thee bail. / But, sirrah, you shall buy this sport as dear / As all the metal in your shop will answer.
I'll obey you till I can pay bail. But you, fellow, will pay as dearly for this game as all the metal in your shop can cover.
Sir, sir, I shall have law in Ephesus, / To your notorious shame, I doubt it not.
Sir, sir, I'll have the law on my side in Ephesus, to your public shame, I don't doubt.

Master, there's a bark of Epidamnum / That stays but till her owner comes aboard, / And then, sir, bears away. Our fraughtage, sir, / I have convey'd aboard, and I have bought / The oil, the balsamum, and aqua-vitae. / The ship is in her trim; the merry wind / Blows fair from land; they stay for nought at all / But for their owner, master, and yourself.

Master, there's a ship from Epidamnum that's only waiting till her owner comes aboard, and then, sir, she sails. I've had our luggage taken aboard, sir, and I've bought the oil, the balsam and the brandy. The ship's ready; a cheerful wind is blowing nicely offshore. They're waiting for nothing at all except their owner, master, and you.
How now? a madman? Why, thou peevish sheep, / What ship of Epidamnum stays for me?
What's this? A madman? Why, you stupid sheep, what ship from Epidamnum is waiting for me?
A ship you sent me to, to hire waftage.
The ship you sent me to, to book our passage.
Thou drunken slave, I sent thee for a rope, / And told thee to what purpose and what end.
You drunken slave, I sent you for a rope, and told you what for and why.
You sent me for a rope's end as soon. / You sent me to the bay, sir, for a bark.
You'd sooner have sent me to be hanged with a rope's end. You sent me to the bay, sir, for a ship.

I will debate this matter at more leisure, / And teach your ears to list me with more heed. / To Adriana, villain, hie thee straight: / Give her this key, and tell her in the desk / That's cover'd o'er with Turkish tapestry / There is a purse of ducats; let her send it. / Tell her I am arrested in the street, / And that shall bail me. Hie thee, slave; be gone. / On, officer, to prison till it come.

I'll argue about this when I've more time, and teach your ears to listen to me more carefully. Go straight to Adriana, you rascal. Give her this key, and tell her that in the desk covered with the Turkish tapestry there's a purse of ducats; she must send it. Tell her I've been arrested in the street, and that will pay my bail. Hurry, slave, go! On to prison, officer, till it comes.

To Adriana, that is where we din'd, / Where Dowsabel did claim me for her husband. / She is too big, I hope, for me to compass. / Thither I must, although against my will, / For servants must their masters' minds fulfil.

To Adriana: that's where we had dinner, where Dowsabel claimed me as her husband. She's too big, I hope, for me to get my arms round. I have to go there, though it's against my will, because servants must carry out their masters' wishes.

Ah, Luciana, did he tempt thee so? / Might'st thou perceive austerely in his eye / That he did plead in earnest, yea or no? / Look'd he or red or pale, or sad or merrily? / What observation mad'st thou in this case / Of his heart's meteors tilting in his face?

Oh, Luciana, did he try to seduce you like that? Could you tell from his eyes, seriously, whether he was pleading in earnest or not? Did he look flushed or pale, serious or cheerful? What did you notice of his heart's passions flashing across his face like meteors?
First he denied you had in him no right.
First he denied that you had any right to him.
He meant he did me none; the more my spite.
He meant he did me no right; all the more spite to me.
Then swore he that he was a stranger here.
Then he swore that he was a stranger here.
And true he swore, though yet forsworn he were.
And he swore the truth, even though he broke his vows.
That love I begg'd for you he begg'd of me.
That he begged me for the love I was begging for you.
With what persuasion did he tempt thy love?
How did he try to win your love?
With words that in an honest suit might move. / First he did praise my beauty, then my speech.
With words that might have moved me if his suit were honest. First he praised my beauty, then my way of speaking.
Did you speak kindly to him?

I cannot, nor I will not hold me still. / My tongue, though not my heart, shall have his will. / He is deformed, crooked, old, and sere, / Ill-fac'd, worse bodied, shapeless everywhere; / Vicious, ungentle, foolish, blunt, unkind, / Stigmatical in making, worse in mind.

I can't keep quiet, and I won't. My tongue, if not my heart, shall have its way. He's deformed, crooked, old and withered, ugly in face and worse in body, misshapen everywhere; wicked, rude, foolish, blunt, unkind, marked by nature as a bad man and worse in his mind.
Who would be jealous then of such a one? / No evil lost is wail'd when it is gone.
Then who would be jealous of someone like that? Nobody mourns the loss of something bad.
Ah, but I think him better than I say, / And yet would herein others' eyes were worse: / Far from her nest the lapwing cries away; / My heart prays for him, though my tongue do curse.

Ah, but I think better of him than I say, and yet I wish other women's eyes thought worse of him. The lapwing cries out far from her nest to draw people away from it: my heart prays for him, though my tongue curses him.
Here, go; the desk, the purse, sweet now, make haste.
Here, go on: the desk, the purse! Sweet lady, hurry now.
How hast thou lost thy breath?
How did you get so out of breath?
Where is thy master, Dromio? is he well?
Where's your master, Dromio? Is he all right?

No, he's in Tartar limbo, worse than hell. / A devil in an everlasting garment hath him, / One whose hard heart is button'd up with steel; / A fiend, a fairy, pitiless and rough; / A wolf, nay worse, a fellow all in buff; / A back-friend, a shoulder-clapper, one that countermands / The passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lands; / A hound that runs counter, and yet draws dryfoot well, / One that, before the judgement, carries poor souls to hell.

No, he's in a hellish jail, worse than hell itself. A devil in a garment that never wears out has got him, one whose hard heart is buttoned up in steel: a fiend, a goblin, pitiless and rough; a wolf, no, worse, a fellow all in leather; a false friend who taps you on the shoulder, one who blocks off alleys, creeks and narrow lanes; a hound that runs the wrong way and yet follows a scent well; one who carries poor souls to hell before their judgement.
Why, man, what is the matter?
I do not know the matter. He is 'rested on the case.
I don't know the matter. He's been arrested on a case.
What, is he arrested? Tell me at whose suit?
What, he's arrested? Tell me, on whose charge?
I know not at whose suit he is arrested, well; / But he's in a suit of buff which 'rested him, that can I tell. / Will you send him, mistress, redemption, the money in his desk?
I don't know on whose charge he's arrested, but he's been arrested by a man in a leather suit, that much I can tell you. Will you send him his redemption, mistress, the money in his desk?
Go fetch it, sister. This I wonder at,
Fetch it, sister. I'm amazed at this,
Thus he unknown to me should be in debt. / Tell me, was he arrested on a band?
that he should be in debt without my knowing. Tell me, was he arrested over a bond?
Not on a band, but on a stronger thing; / A chain, a chain. Do you not hear it ring?
Not over a bond, but over something stronger: a chain, a chain. Can't you hear it ringing?
No, no, the bell, 'tis time that I were gone. / It was two ere I left him, and now the clock strikes one.
No, no, the bell. It's time I was gone. It was two before I left him, and now the clock strikes one.
The hours come back! That did I never hear.
The hours going backwards! I never heard of that.
O yes, if any hour meet a sergeant, 'a turns back for very fear.
Oh yes, if any hour meets a sergeant, it turns back out of pure fear.
As if time were in debt. How fondly dost thou reason!
As if time could be in debt! How foolishly you argue!

Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth to season. / Nay, he's a thief too. Have you not heard men say / That time comes stealing on by night and day? / If he be in debt and theft, and a sergeant in the way, / Hath he not reason to turn back an hour in a day?

Time is completely bankrupt and owes more than he's worth to the occasion. No, he's a thief too. Haven't you heard people say that time comes stealing on, night and day? If he's in debt and a thief, and there's a sergeant in his way, hasn't he reason to turn back an hour in the day?
Go, Dromio, there's the money, bear it straight, / And bring thy master home immediately. / Come, sister, I am press'd down with conceit; / Conceit, my comfort and my injury.
Go, Dromio, there's the money. Take it straight to him, and bring your master home at once. Come, sister, I'm weighed down by my imagination: imagination, my comfort and my injury.

There's not a man I meet but doth salute me / As if I were their well-acquainted friend, / And everyone doth call me by my name. / Some tender money to me, some invite me; / Some other give me thanks for kindnesses; / Some offer me commodities to buy. / Even now a tailor call'd me in his shop, / And show'd me silks that he had bought for me, / And therewithal took measure of my body. / Sure, these are but imaginary wiles, / And Lapland sorcerers inhabit here.

Every man I meet greets me as if I were a close friend, and everyone calls me by my name. Some offer me money, some invite me to their homes, others thank me for kindnesses, some offer me goods to buy. Just now a tailor called me into his shop, showed me silks he had bought for me, and took my measurements as well. Surely these are imaginary tricks, and Lapland sorcerers live here.
Master, here's the gold you sent me for. / What, have you got the picture of old Adam new apparelled?
Master, here's the gold you sent me for. What, have you got rid of the image of old Adam in his new clothes?
What gold is this? What Adam dost thou mean?
What gold is this? What Adam do you mean?

Not that Adam that kept the paradise, but that Adam that keeps the / prison; he that goes in the calf's skin that was killed for the / Prodigal; he that came behind you, sir, like an evil angel, and bid you / forsake your liberty.

Not the Adam who kept paradise, but the Adam who keeps the prison: the one who goes about in the skin of the calf that was killed for the Prodigal Son; the one who came up behind you, sir, like a bad angel, and told you to give up your freedom.

No? Why, 'tis a plain case: he that went like a bass-viol in a case of / leather; the man, sir, that, when gentlemen are tired, gives them a / sob, and 'rests them; he, sir, that takes pity on decayed men and gives / them suits of durance; he that sets up his rest to do more exploits / with his mace than a morris-pike.

No? Why, it's a plain case: the one who went about like a bass viol in a leather case; the man, sir, who, when gentlemen are tired, gives them a tap and arrests them; the one, sir, who takes pity on ruined men and gives them suits that last; the one who's determined to do more damage with his mace than a soldier with a pike.
Ay, sir, the sergeant of the band; he that brings any man to answer it / that breaks his band; one that thinks a man always going to bed, and / says, "God give you good rest."
Yes, sir, the sergeant of the bond: the one who makes any man who breaks his bond answer for it; one who thinks every man is going to bed, and says, "God give you good rest."
Well, sir, there rest in your foolery. Is there any ship puts forth / tonight? may we be gone?
Well, sir, let your foolery rest there. Is there any ship sailing tonight? Can we leave?

Why, sir, I brought you word an hour since that the bark Expedition / put forth tonight, and then were you hindered by the sergeant to tarry / for the hoy Delay. Here are the angels that you sent for to deliver / you.

Why, sir, I told you an hour ago that the ship Expedition was sailing tonight, and then you were held up by the sergeant and had to wait for the barge Delay. Here are the gold angels you sent for to set you free.
The fellow is distract, and so am I, / And here we wander in illusions. / Some blessed power deliver us from hence!
The fellow's out of his mind, and so am I, and we're wandering here among illusions. May some holy power get us out of here!
Well met, well met, Master Antipholus. / I see, sir, you have found the goldsmith now. / Is that the chain you promis'd me today?
Well met, well met, Master Antipholus. I see, sir, you've found the goldsmith at last. Is that the chain you promised me today?
Satan, avoid! I charge thee, tempt me not.
Get behind me, Satan! I order you, don't tempt me.

Nay, she is worse, she is the devil's dam; and here she comes in the / habit of a light wench, and thereof comes that the wenches say "God / damn me", that's as much to say, "God make me a light wench." It is / written they appear to men like angels of light. Light is an effect of / fire, and fire will burn; ergo, light wenches will burn. Come not near / her.

No, she's worse: she's the devil's mother. And here she comes dressed as a light woman, which is why the girls say "God damn me", which is the same as saying "God make me a light woman". It's written that devils appear to men as angels of light. Light comes from fire, and fire burns; so light women will burn. Don't go near her.
Your man and you are marvellous merry, sir. / Will you go with me? We'll mend our dinner here.
You and your man are wonderfully merry, sir. Will you come with me? We'll top up our dinner here.
Master, if you do, expect spoon-meat, or bespeak a long spoon.
Master, if you do, expect soft food eaten with a spoon, or order a long spoon.
Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.
Why, a man needs a long spoon if he's going to eat with the devil.
Avoid then, fiend! What tell'st thou me of supping? / Thou art, as you are all, a sorceress. / I conjure thee to leave me and be gone.
Away then, fiend! Why are you talking to me about supper? You're a sorceress, like all of you here. I command you to leave me and go.
Give me the ring of mine you had at dinner, / Or, for my diamond, the chain you promis'd, / And I'll be gone, sir, and not trouble you.
Give me back my ring you had at dinner, or, in return for my diamond, the chain you promised, and I'll go, sir, and not bother you.

Some devils ask but the paring of one's nail, / A rush, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, / A nut, a cherry-stone; but she, more covetous, / Would have a chain. / Master, be wise; and if you give it her, / The devil will shake her chain and fright us with it.

Some devils only ask for a fingernail clipping, a rush, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherry stone. But she, greedier, wants a chain. Master, be sensible. If you give it to her, the devil will rattle her chain and frighten us with it.
I pray you, sir, my ring, or else the chain; / I hope you do not mean to cheat me so.
Please, sir, my ring, or else the chain. I hope you don't intend to cheat me like this.
Avaunt, thou witch! Come, Dromio, let us go.
Away, you witch! Come, Dromio, let's go.
Fly pride, says the peacock. Mistress, that you know.
"Beware of pride," says the peacock. Mistress, you know all about that.

Now, out of doubt Antipholus is mad, / Else would he never so demean himself. / A ring he hath of mine worth forty ducats, / And for the same he promis'd me a chain; / Both one and other he denies me now. / The reason that I gather he is mad, / Besides this present instance of his rage, / Is a mad tale he told today at dinner / Of his own doors being shut against his entrance. / Belike his wife, acquainted with his fits, / On purpose shut the doors against his way. / My way is now to hie home to his house, / And tell his wife that, being lunatic, / He rush'd into my house and took perforce / My ring away. This course I fittest choose, / For forty ducats is too much to lose.

Now there's no doubt Antipholus is mad, or he would never behave like this. He has a ring of mine worth forty ducats, and in return he promised me a chain. Now he denies me both. Besides this present outburst, what makes me think he's mad is a mad story he told at dinner today about his own doors being shut against him. I suppose his wife, knowing about his fits, shut the doors against him on purpose. My plan now is to hurry to his house and tell his wife that, in a fit of lunacy, he rushed into my house and took my ring by force. This is the best course to take, because forty ducats is too much to lose.

Fear me not, man, I will not break away: / I'll give thee ere I leave thee so much money, / To warrant thee, as I am 'rested for. / My wife is in a wayward mood today, / And will not lightly trust the messenger / That I should be attach'd in Ephesus; / I tell you 'twill sound harshly in her ears.

Don't worry about me, man, I won't run away. Before I leave you I'll give you as much money as I'm arrested for, as your guarantee. My wife is in a difficult mood today and won't easily believe the messenger who says I've been arrested in Ephesus. I tell you, it'll sound harsh in her ears.
Here comes my man. I think he brings the money. / How now, sir! have you that I sent you for?
Here comes my man. I think he's bringing the money. Well, sir! Have you got what I sent you for?
Here's that, I warrant you, will pay them all.
Here's something, I promise you, that will pay them all back.
Why, sir, I gave the money for the rope.
Why, sir, I gave the money for the rope.
Five hundred ducats, villain, for a rope?
Five hundred ducats, you villain, for a rope?
I'll serve you, sir, five hundred at the rate.
I'll get you five hundred ropes at that price, sir.
To what end did I bid thee hie thee home?
What did I tell you to hurry home for?
To a rope's end, sir; and to that end am I return'd.
For a rope's end, sir, and for that end I've come back.
And to that end, sir, I will welcome you.
And for that end, sir, I'll welcome you.
Nay, 'tis for me to be patient. I am in adversity.
No, I'm the one who needs to be patient. I'm the one suffering.
Come on now, hold your tongue.
Nay, rather persuade him to hold his hands.
No, persuade him to hold his hands instead.
You son of a whore, you senseless villain!
I would I were senseless, sir, that I might not feel your blows.
I wish I was senseless, sir, so I couldn't feel your blows.
Thou art sensible in nothing but blows, and so is an ass.
You don't sense anything except blows, and neither does a donkey.

I am an ass indeed; you may prove it by my long ears. I have served him / from the hour of my nativity to this instant, and have nothing at his / hands for my service but blows. When I am cold, he heats me with / beating; when I am warm he cools me with beating. I am waked with it / when I sleep, raised with it when I sit, driven out of doors with it / when I go from home, welcomed home with it when I return. Nay, I bear / it on my shoulders as a beggar wont her brat; and I think when he hath / lamed me, I shall beg with it from door to door.

I'm a donkey all right: you can tell by my long ears. I've served him from the hour I was born till now, and got nothing from him for my service but blows. When I'm cold, he warms me up with a beating; when I'm warm, he cools me down with a beating. I'm woken up with it when I'm asleep, got up with it when I'm sitting down, driven out of the door with it when I go out, welcomed home with it when I come back. Why, I carry it on my shoulders like a beggar woman carries her child, and I think when he's crippled me I'll go begging with it from door to door.
Come, go along, my wife is coming yonder.
Come on, let's go. My wife's coming over there.
Mistress, respice finem, respect your end, or rather, the prophesy / like the parrot, "Beware the rope's end."
Mistress, "respice finem", consider your end; or rather, as the parrot's prophecy goes, "Beware the rope's end."
How say you now? Is not your husband mad?
What do you say now? Isn't your husband mad?
His incivility confirms no less. / Good Doctor Pinch, you are a conjurer; / Establish him in his true sense again, / And I will please you what you will demand.
His violence proves nothing less. Good Doctor Pinch, you know how to cast out spirits. Restore him to his right mind, and I'll pay you whatever you ask.
Alas, how fiery and how sharp he looks!
Oh dear, how wild and fierce he looks!
Mark how he trembles in his ecstasy.
See how he trembles in his fit.
Give me your hand, and let me feel your pulse.
Give me your hand and let me feel your pulse.
There is my hand, and let it feel your ear.
There's my hand, and let it feel your ear.
I charge thee, Satan, hous'd within this man, / To yield possession to my holy prayers, / And to thy state of darkness hie thee straight. / I conjure thee by all the saints in heaven.
I command you, Satan, living inside this man, to give up your hold to my holy prayers and hurry straight back to your realm of darkness. I command you by all the saints in heaven.
Peace, doting wizard, peace; I am not mad.
Quiet, you senile wizard, quiet! I'm not mad.
O, that thou wert not, poor distressed soul!
Oh, if only you weren't, poor troubled soul!

You minion, you, are these your customers? / Did this companion with the saffron face / Revel and feast it at my house today, / Whilst upon me the guilty doors were shut, / And I denied to enter in my house?
You hussy, are these your clients? Did this fellow with the yellow face party and feast at my house today, while the guilty doors were shut on me and I was refused entry to my own house?
O husband, God doth know you din'd at home, / Where would you had remain'd until this time, / Free from these slanders and this open shame.
Oh husband, God knows you dined at home, and I wish you'd stayed there till now, free from these slanders and this public shame.
Din'd at home? Thou villain, what sayest thou?
Dined at home? You villain, what do you say?
Sir, sooth to say, you did not dine at home.
Sir, to tell the truth, you didn't dine at home.
Were not my doors lock'd up and I shut out?
Weren't my doors locked and I shut out?
Perdy, your doors were lock'd, and you shut out.
By God, your doors were locked, and you were shut out.
And did not she herself revile me there?
And didn't she herself abuse me there?
Sans fable, she herself revil'd you there.
No word of a lie, she abused you there herself.
Did not her kitchen-maid rail, taunt, and scorn me?
Didn't her kitchen maid rail at me, taunt me and scorn me?
Certes, she did, the kitchen-vestal scorn'd you.
Certainly she did: the kitchen-goddess scorned you.
And did not I in rage depart from thence?
And didn't I leave there in a rage?
In verity, you did; my bones bear witness, / That since have felt the vigour of his rage.
In truth you did. My bones can bear witness, since they've felt the force of his rage ever since.
Is't good to soothe him in these contraries?
Is it a good idea to humour him in these contradictions?
It is no shame; the fellow finds his vein, / And yielding to him, humours well his frenzy.
There's no harm in it. The fellow has worked out his mood, and by agreeing with him, he's humouring his madness well.
Thou hast suborn'd the goldsmith to arrest me.
You've bribed the goldsmith to have me arrested.
Alas! I sent you money to redeem you / By Dromio here, who came in haste for it.
Oh! I sent you money to free you, by Dromio here, who came rushing for it.
Money by me? Heart and goodwill you might, / But surely, master, not a rag of money.
Money by me? Love and goodwill maybe, but certainly, master, not a scrap of money.
Went'st not thou to her for a purse of ducats?
Didn't you go to her for a purse of ducats?
He came to me, and I deliver'd it.
He came to me, and I gave it to him.
And I am witness with her that she did.
And I'm a witness with her that she did.
God and the rope-maker bear me witness / That I was sent for nothing but a rope.
God and the rope-maker are my witnesses that I was sent for nothing but a rope.
Mistress, both man and master is possess'd, / I know it by their pale and deadly looks. / They must be bound and laid in some dark room.
Mistress, both man and master are possessed. I can tell by their pale, deathly looks. They must be tied up and put in some dark room.
Say, wherefore didst thou lock me forth today, / And why dost thou deny the bag of gold?
Tell me, why did you lock me out today, and why do you deny the bag of gold?
I did not, gentle husband, lock thee forth.
I didn't lock you out, dear husband.
And gentle master, I receiv'd no gold; / But I confess, sir, that we were lock'd out.
And dear master, I received no gold. But I admit, sir, that we were locked out.
Dissembling villain, thou speak'st false in both.
Lying villain, you're lying in both.

Dissembling harlot, thou art false in all, / And art confederate with a damned pack / To make a loathsome abject scorn of me. / But with these nails I'll pluck out these false eyes / That would behold in me this shameful sport.

Lying whore, you're false in everything, and in league with a damned gang to make me a disgusting object of scorn. But I'll pluck out those false eyes with these nails, for wanting to see me made a shameful joke.
O, bind him, bind him; let him not come near me.
Oh, tie him up, tie him up! Don't let him near me.
More company; the fiend is strong within him.
More men! The devil is strong in him.
Ay me, poor man, how pale and wan he looks!
Oh dear, poor man, how pale and sickly he looks!
What, will you murder me? Thou jailer, thou, / I am thy prisoner. Wilt thou suffer them / To make a rescue?
What, will you murder me? You, jailer, I'm your prisoner. Will you let them snatch me from you?
Masters, let him go. / He is my prisoner, and you shall not have him.
Gentlemen, let him go. He's my prisoner, and you can't have him.
Go, bind this man, for he is frantic too.
Go and tie up this man too, because he's raving as well.
What wilt thou do, thou peevish officer? / Hast thou delight to see a wretched man / Do outrage and displeasure to himself?
What do you think you're doing, you stubborn officer? Do you enjoy seeing a wretched man do himself violence and harm?
He is my prisoner. If I let him go, / The debt he owes will be requir'd of me.
He's my prisoner. If I let him go, I'll be made to pay the debt he owes.

I will discharge thee ere I go from thee; / Bear me forthwith unto his creditor, / And knowing how the debt grows, I will pay it. / Good master doctor, see him safe convey'd / Home to my house. O most unhappy day!

I'll settle with you before I leave you. Take me straight to his creditor, and once I know how the debt arose, I'll pay it. Good master doctor, see that he's taken safely home to my house. Oh, most unhappy day!
Master, I am here enter'd in bond for you.
Master, I've been tied up here on your account.
Out on thee, villain! wherefore dost thou mad me?
Damn you, villain! Why are you driving me mad?
Will you be bound for nothing? Be mad, good master; cry, "the devil".
Will you be tied up for nothing? Go mad, good master: shout "the devil!"
God help, poor souls, how idly do they talk!
God help them, poor souls, what nonsense they talk!
Go bear him hence. Sister, go you with me.
Take him away. Sister, you come with me.
Say now, whose suit is he arrested at?
Now tell me, on whose claim was he arrested?
One Angelo, a goldsmith; do you know him?
A man called Angelo, a goldsmith. Do you know him?
I know the man. What is the sum he owes?
I know the man. How much does my husband owe?
Due for a chain your husband had of him.
For a chain your husband had from him.
He did bespeak a chain for me, but had it not.
He did order a chain for me, but he never got it.
When as your husband, all in rage, today / Came to my house and took away my ring, / The ring I saw upon his finger now, / Straight after did I meet him with a chain.
When your husband came to my house today in a rage and took away my ring, the ring I saw on his finger just now, straight afterwards I met him with a chain.
It may be so, but I did never see it. / Come, jailer, bring me where the goldsmith is, / I long to know the truth hereof at large.
That may be, but I never saw it. Come, jailer, take me to the goldsmith. I'm longing to know the whole truth of this.
God, for thy mercy, they are loose again!
God have mercy, they've got loose again!
And come with naked swords. Let's call more help / To have them bound again.
And they're coming with swords drawn! Let's call more help to tie them up again.
I see these witches are afraid of swords.
I see these witches are afraid of swords.
She that would be your wife now ran from you.
The woman who wanted to be your wife has just run away from you.
Come to the Centaur, fetch our stuff from thence. / I long that we were safe and sound aboard.
Go to the Centaur and fetch our luggage from there. I can't wait to be safe and sound on board.

Faith, stay here this night, they will surely do us no harm; you saw / they speak us fair, give us gold. Methinks they are such a gentle / nation that, but for the mountain of mad flesh that claims marriage of / me, I could find in my heart to stay here still and turn witch.

Honestly, let's stay here tonight. They certainly won't harm us: you saw they speak kindly to us and give us gold. I think they're such a gentle nation that, if it wasn't for the mountain of mad flesh who claims me in marriage, I could find it in my heart to stay here for good and become a witch.
I will not stay tonight for all the town; / Therefore away, to get our stuff aboard.
I wouldn't stay tonight for the whole town. So come on, let's get our luggage aboard.
I am sorry, sir, that I have hinder'd you, / But I protest he had the chain of me, / Though most dishonestly he doth deny it.
I'm sorry, sir, that I've held you up, but I swear he had the chain from me, though he very dishonestly denies it.
How is the man esteem'd here in the city?
What do people think of the man here in the city?
Of very reverend reputation, sir, / Of credit infinite, highly belov'd, / Second to none that lives here in the city. / His word might bear my wealth at any time.
He has a very respected reputation, sir, unlimited credit, he's much loved, second to no one living in this city. His word would be good for all my wealth at any time.
Speak softly. Yonder, as I think, he walks.
Speak quietly. I think that's him walking over there.

'Tis so; and that self chain about his neck / Which he forswore most monstrously to have. / Good sir, draw near to me, I'll speak to him. / Signior Antipholus, I wonder much / That you would put me to this shame and trouble, / And not without some scandal to yourself, / With circumstance and oaths so to deny / This chain, which now you wear so openly. / Beside the charge, the shame, imprisonment, / You have done wrong to this my honest friend, / Who, but for staying on our controversy, / Had hoisted sail and put to sea today. / This chain you had of me, can you deny it?

It is, and wearing round his neck the very chain he so outrageously swore he never had. Good sir, come closer to me. I'll speak to him. Signor Antipholus, I'm amazed that you would put me to such shame and trouble, and not without some scandal to yourself, by denying so elaborately and with such oaths this chain that you're now wearing so openly. Besides the cost, the shame and the arrest, you've wronged my honest friend here, who would have set sail and put out to sea today if he hadn't stayed for our dispute. You had this chain from me: can you deny it?
I think I had: I never did deny it.
I think I did. I never denied it.
Yes, that you did, sir, and forswore it too.
Yes, you did, sir, and swore falsely about it too.
Who heard me to deny it or forswear it?
Who heard me deny it or swear falsely?
These ears of mine, thou know'st, did hear thee. / Fie on thee, wretch. 'Tis pity that thou liv'st / To walk where any honest men resort.
These ears of mine heard you, as you know. Shame on you, wretch! It's a pity you're alive to walk where honest men go.
Thou art a villain to impeach me thus; / I'll prove mine honour and mine honesty / Against thee presently, if thou dar'st stand.
You're a villain to accuse me like this. I'll prove my honour and honesty against you right now, if you dare to stand and fight.
I dare, and do defy thee for a villain.
I dare, and I challenge you as a villain.
Hold, hurt him not, for God's sake, he is mad. / Some get within him, take his sword away. / Bind Dromio too, and bear them to my house.
Stop, don't hurt him, for God's sake! He's mad. Someone get close to him and take his sword away. Tie up Dromio too, and carry them to my house.
Run, master, run, for God's sake, take a house. / This is some priory; in, or we are spoil'd.
Run, master, run, for God's sake! Get inside a building. This is some priory. In, or we're done for!
Be quiet, people. Wherefore throng you hither?
Quiet, everyone. Why are you crowding here?
To fetch my poor distracted husband hence. / Let us come in, that we may bind him fast / And bear him home for his recovery.
To fetch my poor, deranged husband from here. Let us in, so we can tie him up securely and take him home to recover.
I knew he was not in his perfect wits.
I knew he wasn't in his right mind.
I am sorry now that I did draw on him.
Now I'm sorry I drew my sword on him.
How long hath this possession held the man?
How long has this fit held the man?
This week he hath been heavy, sour, sad, / And much different from the man he was. / But till this afternoon his passion / Ne'er brake into extremity of rage.
All this week he's been heavy, sour and sad, and very different from the man he used to be. But until this afternoon his disorder never broke out into such extreme rage.

Hath he not lost much wealth by wreck of sea? / Buried some dear friend? Hath not else his eye / Stray'd his affection in unlawful love? / A sin prevailing much in youthful men / Who give their eyes the liberty of gazing? / Which of these sorrows is he subject to?

Hasn't he lost a lot of money in a shipwreck? Buried some dear friend? Or has his eye led his affections astray into unlawful love, a sin very common in young men who let their eyes wander freely? Which of these sorrows is he suffering from?
To none of these, except it be the last, / Namely, some love that drew him oft from home.
None of these, unless it's the last: some love that often drew him away from home.
You should for that have reprehended him.
You should have scolded him for that.
As roughly as my modesty would let me.
As harshly as my modesty would let me.

It was the copy of our conference. / In bed he slept not for my urging it; / At board he fed not for my urging it; / Alone, it was the subject of my theme; / In company I often glanced it; / Still did I tell him it was vile and bad.

It was the theme of all our conversation. In bed, he couldn't sleep because I kept on about it. At the table, he couldn't eat because I kept on about it. Alone, it was the subject I talked about; in company, I often hinted at it. I always told him it was vile and wicked.

And thereof came it that the man was mad. / The venom clamours of a jealous woman / Poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth. / It seems his sleeps were hindered by thy railing, / And thereof comes it that his head is light. / Thou say'st his meat was sauc'd with thy upbraidings. / Unquiet meals make ill digestions; / Thereof the raging fire of fever bred, / And what's a fever but a fit of madness? / Thou say'st his sports were hinder'd by thy brawls. / Sweet recreation barr'd, what doth ensue / But moody and dull melancholy, / Kinsman to grim and comfortless despair, / And at her heels a huge infectious troop / Of pale distemperatures and foes to life? / In food, in sport, and life-preserving rest / To be disturb'd would mad or man or beast. / The consequence is, then, thy jealous fits / Hath scar'd thy husband from the use of's wits.

And that's how the man came to be mad. The venomous ranting of a jealous woman poisons more deadly than a mad dog's bite. It seems your nagging kept him from sleeping, and that's why his head is light. You say his food was seasoned with your scolding. Disturbed meals make for bad digestion; that breeds the raging fire of fever, and what is fever but a fit of madness? You say your quarrelling spoiled his pleasures. When sweet recreation is barred, what follows but moody, dull melancholy, close relative of grim, comfortless despair, followed by a huge infectious troop of pale diseases that are enemies to life? Being disturbed in food, in pleasure and in life-giving sleep would drive man or beast mad. The result is that your jealous fits have frightened your husband out of his wits.
She never reprehended him but mildly, / When he demean'd himself rough, rude, and wildly. / Why bear you these rebukes and answer not?
She only ever scolded him gently, when he behaved roughly, rudely and wildly. Why do you take these rebukes and not answer back?
She did betray me to my own reproof. / Good people, enter and lay hold on him.
She has tricked me into blaming myself. Good people, go in and seize him.
No, not a creature enters in my house.
No, not one creature enters my house.
Then let your servants bring my husband forth.
Then let your servants bring my husband out.
Neither. He took this place for sanctuary, / And it shall privilege him from your hands / Till I have brought him to his wits again, / Or lose my labour in assaying it.
Neither. He took this place as a sanctuary, and it will protect him from your hands until I've brought him back to his senses, or wasted my efforts trying.
I will attend my husband, be his nurse, / Diet his sickness, for it is my office, / And will have no attorney but myself; / And therefore let me have him home with me.
I'll look after my husband, nurse him and treat his sickness, because it's my duty. I'll have no one act for me but myself, so let me take him home with me.

Be patient, for I will not let him stir / Till I have used the approved means I have, / With wholesome syrups, drugs, and holy prayers, / To make of him a formal man again. / It is a branch and parcel of mine oath, / A charitable duty of my order; / Therefore depart, and leave him here with me.

Be patient, because I won't let him stir until I've used the tested remedies I have, healthy syrups, drugs and holy prayers, to make him a normal man again. It is part of my vows, a charitable duty of my order. So go, and leave him here with me.
I will not hence and leave my husband here; / And ill it doth beseem your holiness / To separate the husband and the wife.
I won't go away and leave my husband here. And it ill becomes your holiness to separate husband and wife.
Be quiet and depart. Thou shalt not have him.
Be quiet and go. You will not have him.
Complain unto the duke of this indignity.
Complain to the Duke about this outrage.
Come, go. I will fall prostrate at his feet, / And never rise until my tears and prayers / Have won his grace to come in person hither / And take perforce my husband from the abbess.
Come, let's go. I'll throw myself at his feet and never get up until my tears and prayers have persuaded his grace to come here himself and take my husband from the abbess by force.

By this, I think, the dial points at five. / Anon, I'm sure, the Duke himself in person / Comes this way to the melancholy vale, / The place of death and sorry execution / Behind the ditches of the abbey here.
I think by now the sundial points to five. Soon, I'm sure, the Duke himself will come this way to the gloomy valley, the place of death and sad executions behind the abbey ditches here.
To see a reverend Syracusian merchant, / Who put unluckily into this bay / Against the laws and statutes of this town, / Beheaded publicly for his offence.
To see a respected merchant from Syracuse, who unluckily came into this bay against the laws and statutes of this town, publicly beheaded for his offence.
See where they come. We will behold his death.
Look, here they come. We'll watch his death.
Kneel to the Duke before he pass the abbey.
Kneel to the Duke before he passes the abbey.
Yet once again proclaim it publicly, / If any friend will pay the sum for him, / He shall not die; so much we tender him.
Announce it publicly once more: if any friend will pay the sum for him, he will not die. That's how much we care for him.
Justice, most sacred duke, against the abbess!
Justice, most sacred Duke, against the abbess!
She is a virtuous and a reverend lady, / It cannot be that she hath done thee wrong.
She is a virtuous and respected lady. It can't be that she has wronged you.

May it please your grace, Antipholus, my husband, / Who I made lord of me and all I had / At your important letters, this ill day / A most outrageous fit of madness took him; / That desp'rately he hurried through the street, / With him his bondman all as mad as he, / Doing displeasure to the citizens / By rushing in their houses, bearing thence / Rings, jewels, anything his rage did like. / Once did I get him bound and sent him home, / Whilst to take order for the wrongs I went, / That here and there his fury had committed. / Anon, I wot not by what strong escape, / He broke from those that had the guard of him, / And with his mad attendant and himself, / Each one with ireful passion, with drawn swords, / Met us again, and, madly bent on us, / Chased us away; till raising of more aid, / We came again to bind them. Then they fled / Into this abbey, whither we pursued them. / And here the abbess shuts the gates on us, / And will not suffer us to fetch him out, / Nor send him forth that we may bear him hence. / Therefore, most gracious duke, with thy command / Let him be brought forth and borne hence for help.

May it please your grace: Antipholus, my husband, whom I made lord of myself and all I owned at your urgent request, was seized by a most outrageous fit of madness on this bad day. He rushed wildly through the street, with his servant just as mad as he, offending the citizens by bursting into their houses and carrying off rings, jewels, anything his rage fancied. Once I had him tied up and sent home, while I went to settle the damage his fury had done here and there. Then, by I don't know what violent escape, he broke away from the men guarding him, and he and his mad servant, both furious, with drawn swords, met us again, came madly at us and chased us away, until we raised more help and came back to tie them up. Then they fled into this abbey, where we chased them. And here the abbess shuts the gates on us and won't let us fetch him out, or send him out so we can take him away. So, most gracious Duke, at your command let him be brought out and taken away for help.

Long since thy husband serv'd me in my wars, / And I to thee engag'd a prince's word, / When thou didst make him master of thy bed, / To do him all the grace and good I could. / Go, some of you, knock at the abbey gate, / And bid the lady abbess come to me. / I will determine this before I stir.

Long ago your husband served me in my wars, and when you made him your husband I gave you my word as a prince to do him all the favour and good I could. Some of you, go and knock at the abbey gate and tell the lady abbess to come to me. I'll settle this before I move.

O mistress, mistress, shift and save yourself. / My master and his man are both broke loose, / Beaten the maids a-row, and bound the doctor, / Whose beard they have singed off with brands of fire, / And ever as it blazed they threw on him / Great pails of puddled mire to quench the hair. / My master preaches patience to him, and the while / His man with scissors nicks him like a fool; / And sure (unless you send some present help) / Between them they will kill the conjurer.

Oh mistress, mistress, run and save yourself! My master and his man have both broken loose, beaten the maids one after another and tied up the doctor. They've singed his beard off with burning sticks, and every time it caught fire they threw great buckets of muddy water on him to put his hair out. My master preaches patience to him, while his man cuts his hair with scissors like a fool's. Surely, unless you send help at once, between them they'll kill the conjuror.
Peace, fool, thy master and his man are here, / And that is false thou dost report to us.
Quiet, fool. Your master and his man are here, and what you're telling us is false.
Mistress, upon my life, I tell you true. / I have not breath'd almost since I did see it. / He cries for you, and vows, if he can take you, / To scorch your face and to disfigure you.
Mistress, on my life, I'm telling the truth. I've hardly taken a breath since I saw it. He's shouting for you and swears that if he catches you he'll scorch your face and disfigure you.
Hark, hark, I hear him, mistress. Fly, be gone!
Listen, listen, I can hear him, mistress. Run, go!
Come, stand by me, fear nothing. Guard with halberds.
Come, stand by me, don't be afraid. Guard us with your halberds.
Ay me, it is my husband. Witness you / That he is borne about invisible. / Even now we hous'd him in the abbey here, / And now he's there, past thought of human reason.
Oh dear, it's my husband! You're witnesses that he is being carried about invisibly. A moment ago we drove him into the abbey here, and now he's there, beyond anything human reason can explain.

Justice, most gracious duke; O, grant me justice! / Even for the service that long since I did thee / When I bestrid thee in the wars, and took / Deep scars to save thy life; even for the blood / That then I lost for thee, now grant me justice.

Justice, most gracious Duke, oh, grant me justice! For the sake of the service I did you long ago, when I stood over you in battle and took deep wounds to save your life, for the sake of the blood I lost for you then, grant me justice now.
Unless the fear of death doth make me dote, / I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.
Unless the fear of death is making me see things, I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.

Justice, sweet prince, against that woman there. / She whom thou gav'st to me to be my wife; / That hath abused and dishonour'd me / Even in the strength and height of injury. / Beyond imagination is the wrong / That she this day hath shameless thrown on me.

Justice, sweet prince, against that woman there, the one you gave me as my wife, who has abused and dishonoured me with the most extreme injury. The wrong she has shamelessly done me today is beyond imagining.
Discover how, and thou shalt find me just.
Reveal how, and you'll find me just.
This day, great duke, she shut the doors upon me / While she with harlots feasted in my house.
Today, great Duke, she shut the doors on me while she feasted with lowlifes in my house.
A grievous fault. Say, woman, didst thou so?
A serious offence. Tell me, woman, did you do that?
No, my good lord. Myself, he, and my sister / Today did dine together. So befall my soul / As this is false he burdens me withal.
No, my good lord. He, my sister and I dined together today. May my soul suffer if what he accuses me of isn't false.
Ne'er may I look on day nor sleep on night / But she tells to your highness simple truth.
May I never see daylight or sleep at night again if she isn't telling your highness the plain truth.
O perjur'd woman! They are both forsworn. / In this the madman justly chargeth them.
Oh, lying woman! They're both perjuring themselves. In this the madman accuses them rightly.

My liege, I am advised what I say, / Neither disturb'd with the effect of wine, / Nor heady-rash, provok'd with raging ire, / Albeit my wrongs might make one wiser mad. / This woman lock'd me out this day from dinner. / That goldsmith there, were he not pack'd with her, / Could witness it, for he was with me then, / Who parted with me to go fetch a chain, / Promising to bring it to the Porpentine, / Where Balthasar and I did dine together. / Our dinner done, and he not coming thither, / I went to seek him. In the street I met him, / And in his company that gentleman. / There did this perjur'd goldsmith swear me down / That I this day of him receiv'd the chain, / Which, God he knows, I saw not. For the which / He did arrest me with an officer. / I did obey, and sent my peasant home / For certain ducats. He with none return'd. / Then fairly I bespoke the officer / To go in person with me to my house. / By th' way we met / My wife, her sister, and a rabble more / Of vile confederates. Along with them / They brought one Pinch, a hungry lean-faced villain, / A mere anatomy, a mountebank, / A threadbare juggler, and a fortune-teller; / A needy, hollow-ey'd, sharp-looking wretch; / A living dead man. This pernicious slave, / Forsooth, took on him as a conjurer, / And gazing in mine eyes, feeling my pulse, / And with no face (as 'twere) outfacing me, / Cries out, I was possess'd. Then altogether / They fell upon me, bound me, bore me thence, / And in a dark and dankish vault at home / There left me and my man, both bound together, / Till gnawing with my teeth my bonds in sunder, / I gain'd my freedom and immediately / Ran hither to your Grace, whom I beseech / To give me ample satisfaction / For these deep shames and great indignities.

My lord, I know what I'm saying. I'm not affected by wine, or rash and hot-headed with raging anger, though my wrongs might drive a wiser man mad. This woman locked me out from dinner today. That goldsmith there, if he weren't in league with her, could confirm it, because he was with me then. He left me to fetch a chain, promising to bring it to the Porcupine, where Balthasar and I had dinner together. When dinner was over and he hadn't come, I went to look for him. I met him in the street, with that gentleman in his company. There this lying goldsmith swore to my face that I had received the chain from him today, which, God knows, I never saw. For that he had me arrested by an officer. I obeyed, and sent my slave home for some ducats. He came back with none. Then I politely asked the officer to come with me to my house himself. On the way we met my wife, her sister and a whole rabble of vile accomplices. They brought along one Pinch, a hungry, lean-faced villain, a walking skeleton, a quack, a threadbare conjurer and fortune-teller, a needy, hollow-eyed, sharp-faced wretch, a living dead man. This poisonous slave, if you please, set himself up as an exorcist, and gazing into my eyes, feeling my pulse, and staring me down with his non-existent face, as it were, cried out that I was possessed. Then they all fell on me together, tied me up, carried me off, and left me and my man tied together in a dark, damp cellar at home, until I gnawed through my bonds with my teeth, won my freedom and ran straight here to your grace. I beg you to give me full satisfaction for these deep humiliations and great insults.
My lord, in truth, thus far I witness with him, / That he din'd not at home, but was lock'd out.
My lord, truly, I can confirm this much: he didn't dine at home, but was locked out.
But had he such a chain of thee, or no?
But did he have such a chain from you or not?
He had, my lord, and when he ran in here / These people saw the chain about his neck.
He did, my lord, and when he ran in here these people saw the chain round his neck.

Besides, I will be sworn these ears of mine / Heard you confess you had the chain of him, / After you first forswore it on the mart, / And thereupon I drew my sword on you; / And then you fled into this abbey here, / From whence I think you are come by miracle.

Besides, I'll swear these ears of mine heard you admit you had the chain from him, after you first denied it at the market, and at that I drew my sword on you. Then you fled into this abbey here, and I think you've come out of it by a miracle.
I never came within these abbey walls, / Nor ever didst thou draw thy sword on me. / I never saw the chain, so help me heaven; / And this is false you burden me withal.
I never came inside these abbey walls, and you never drew your sword on me. I never saw the chain, so help me heaven, and what you accuse me of is false.

Why, what an intricate impeach is this! / I think you all have drunk of Circe's cup. / If here you hous'd him, here he would have been. / If he were mad, he would not plead so coldly. / You say he din'd at home, the goldsmith here / Denies that saying. Sirrah, what say you?

Why, what a tangled accusation this is! I think you've all drunk from Circe's cup. If you drove him in here, he'd be in here. If he were mad, he wouldn't plead so calmly. You say he dined at home; the goldsmith here denies it. Fellow, what do you say?
Sir, he dined with her there, at the Porpentine.
Sir, he dined with her there, at the Porcupine.
He did, and from my finger snatch'd that ring.
He did, and snatched that ring off my finger.
'Tis true, my liege, this ring I had of her.
It's true, my lord. I had this ring from her.
Saw'st thou him enter at the abbey here?
Did you see him go into the abbey here?
As sure, my liege, as I do see your grace.
As surely, my lord, as I see your grace.
Why, this is strange. Go call the abbess hither. / I think you are all mated, or stark mad.
Why, this is strange. Go and call the abbess here. I think you're all bewildered, or stark mad.
Most mighty Duke, vouchsafe me speak a word; / Haply I see a friend will save my life / And pay the sum that may deliver me.
Most mighty Duke, allow me to say a word. By luck I see a friend who will save my life and pay the sum that will free me.
Speak freely, Syracusian, what thou wilt.
Speak freely, man of Syracuse. Say what you want.
Is not your name, sir, call'd Antipholus? / And is not that your bondman Dromio?
Isn't your name Antipholus, sir? And isn't that your servant Dromio?
Within this hour I was his bondman, sir, / But he, I thank him, gnaw'd in two my cords. / Now am I Dromio, and his man, unbound.
An hour ago I was his bondman, sir, but he, thank him, gnawed my cords in two. Now I'm Dromio, his man, unbound.
I am sure you both of you remember me.
I'm sure you both remember me.
Ourselves we do remember, sir, by you. / For lately we were bound as you are now. / You are not Pinch's patient, are you, sir?
We're reminded of ourselves, sir, by looking at you, because we were bound just now as you are. You're not one of Pinch's patients, are you, sir?
Why look you strange on me? you know me well.
Why do you look at me like a stranger? You know me well.
I never saw you in my life till now.
I never saw you in my life till now.
O! grief hath chang'd me since you saw me last, / And careful hours with time's deformed hand, / Have written strange defeatures in my face. / But tell me yet, dost thou not know my voice?
Oh, grief has changed me since you saw me last, and anxious hours, with time's disfiguring hand, have written strange changes on my face. But tell me, don't you know my voice?
No, trust me, sir, nor I.
No, believe me, sir, I don't.
Ay, sir, but I am sure I do not, and whatsoever a man denies, you are / now bound to believe him.
Yes, sir, but I'm sure I don't; and whatever a man denies, you're now bound to believe him.

Not know my voice! O time's extremity, / Hast thou so crack'd and splitted my poor tongue / In seven short years that here my only son / Knows not my feeble key of untun'd cares? / Though now this grained face of mine be hid / In sap-consuming winter's drizzled snow, / And all the conduits of my blood froze up, / Yet hath my night of life some memory, / My wasting lamps some fading glimmer left, / My dull deaf ears a little use to hear. / All these old witnesses, I cannot err, / Tell me thou art my son Antipholus.

Not know my voice! Oh, cruel time, have you so cracked and split my poor voice in seven short years that my only son here doesn't know my feeble, worn-out tone? Though my lined face is now hidden under the drizzling snow of winter, which dries up life, and all the channels of my blood are frozen, my life's night still has some memory, my dimming eyes some glimmer of light, my dull, deaf ears a little hearing. All these old witnesses tell me, and I can't be wrong, that you are my son Antipholus.
I never saw my father in my life.
I never saw my father in my life.
But seven years since, in Syracusa, boy, / Thou know'st we parted; but perhaps, my son, / Thou sham'st to acknowledge me in misery.
But you know we parted in Syracuse only seven years ago, boy. Or perhaps, my son, you're ashamed to acknowledge me in my misery.
The duke and all that know me in the city, / Can witness with me that it is not so. / I ne'er saw Syracusa in my life.
The Duke and everyone who knows me in the city can bear witness that it's not so. I've never seen Syracuse in my life.
I tell thee, Syracusian, twenty years / Have I been patron to Antipholus, / During which time he ne'er saw Syracusa. / I see thy age and dangers make thee dote.
I tell you, man of Syracuse, I have been Antipholus's patron for twenty years, and in that time he has never seen Syracuse. I see your age and danger make you rave.
Most mighty duke, behold a man much wrong'd.
Most mighty Duke, look at a man who has been badly wronged.
I see two husbands, or mine eyes deceive me.
I see two husbands, or my eyes deceive me.
One of these men is genius to the other; / And so of these, which is the natural man, / And which the spirit? Who deciphers them?
One of these men is the other's guardian spirit, and the same with these two. Which is the real man, and which the spirit? Who can tell them apart?
I, sir, am Dromio, command him away.
I, sir, am Dromio. Order him away.
I, sir, am Dromio, pray let me stay.
I, sir, am Dromio. Please let me stay.
Egeon, art thou not? or else his ghost?
Aren't you Egeon? Or else his ghost?
O, my old master, who hath bound him here?
Oh, my old master! Who has tied him up here?

Whoever bound him, I will loose his bonds, / And gain a husband by his liberty. / Speak, old Egeon, if thou be'st the man / That hadst a wife once called Emilia, / That bore thee at a burden two fair sons. / O, if thou be'st the same Egeon, speak, / And speak unto the same Emilia!

Whoever tied him up, I will untie his bonds and win back a husband by freeing him. Speak, old Egeon, if you're the man who once had a wife called Emilia, who bore you two fine sons at one birth. Oh, if you're that same Egeon, speak, and speak to that same Emilia!

Why, here begins his morning story right: / These two Antipholus', these two so like, / And these two Dromios, one in semblance, / Besides her urging of her wreck at sea. / These are the parents to these children, / Which accidentally are met together.

Why, here his story from this morning begins to come right. These two Antipholuses, so alike, and these two Dromios, identical in looks, besides what she says about her shipwreck: these are the parents of these children, who have met together by chance.
If I dream not, thou art Emilia. / If thou art she, tell me where is that son / That floated with thee on the fatal raft?
If I'm not dreaming, you are Emilia. If you are, tell me, where is the son who floated with you on that fatal raft?

By men of Epidamnum, he and I / And the twin Dromio, all were taken up; / But, by and by, rude fishermen of Corinth / By force took Dromio and my son from them, / And me they left with those of Epidamnum. / What then became of them I cannot tell; / I to this fortune that you see me in.

He and I and the twin Dromio were all picked up by men from Epidamnum. But soon after, rough fishermen from Corinth took Dromio and my son from them by force, and left me with the men of Epidamnum. What became of them after that I can't tell. I came to the life you see me in now.
Antipholus, thou cam'st from Corinth first?
Antipholus, you came from Corinth originally?
No, sir, not I, I came from Syracuse.
No, sir, not me. I came from Syracuse.
Stay, stand apart, I know not which is which.
Wait, stand apart. I don't know which is which.
I came from Corinth, my most gracious lord.
I came from Corinth, my most gracious lord.
Brought to this town by that most famous warrior, / Duke Menaphon, your most renowned uncle.
Brought to this town by that most famous warrior, Duke Menaphon, your much celebrated uncle.
Which of you two did dine with me today?
Which of you two had dinner with me today?
And are not you my husband?
No, I say nay to that.
No, I say no to that.

And so do I, yet did she call me so; / And this fair gentlewoman, her sister here, / Did call me brother. What I told you then, / I hope I shall have leisure to make good, / If this be not a dream I see and hear.

And so do I, though she called me that, and this lovely lady, her sister here, called me brother. (To Luciana) I hope I'll have time to make good what I told you then, if this isn't a dream I'm seeing and hearing.
That is the chain, sir, which you had of me.
That is the chain, sir, that you had from me.
I think it be, sir. I deny it not.
I think it is, sir. I don't deny it.
And you, sir, for this chain arrested me.
And you, sir, had me arrested for this chain.
I think I did, sir. I deny it not.
I think I did, sir. I don't deny it.
I sent you money, sir, to be your bail / By Dromio, but I think he brought it not.
I sent you money for your bail, sir, by Dromio, but I think he didn't bring it.

This purse of ducats I receiv'd from you, / And Dromio my man did bring them me. / I see we still did meet each other's man, / And I was ta'en for him, and he for me, / And thereupon these errors are arose.

I received this purse of ducats from you, and my man Dromio brought it to me. I see we kept meeting each other's servant, and I was taken for him, and he for me, and that's how these errors came about.
These ducats pawn I for my father here.
I offer these ducats as ransom for my father here.
It shall not need, thy father hath his life.
There's no need. Your father's life is spared.
Sir, I must have that diamond from you.
Sir, I must have that diamond back from you.
There, take it, and much thanks for my good cheer.
There, take it, and many thanks for my good meal.

Renowned duke, vouchsafe to take the pains / To go with us into the abbey here, / And hear at large discoursed all our fortunes; / And all that are assembled in this place, / That by this sympathised one day's error / Have suffer'd wrong, go, keep us company, / And we shall make full satisfaction. / Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail / Of you, my sons, and till this present hour / My heavy burden ne'er delivered. / The duke, my husband, and my children both, / And you, the calendars of their nativity, / Go to a gossips' feast, and go with me. / After so long grief, such nativity.

Renowned Duke, please be good enough to come with us into the abbey here and hear the full story of all our fortunes. And all of you gathered here who have suffered wrong through the shared errors of this one day, come and keep us company, and we will make full amends. For thirty-three years I have been in labour with you, my sons, and only at this hour have I been delivered of my heavy burden. The Duke, my husband and both my children, and you two, born on the same day as them, come to a christening feast, come with me. After such long grief, such a birth!
